course.title: Economics: Markets and Strategy
course.description: Price a trade-off, find where supply meets demand, weigh a tax and outguess a rival. Every idea is worked with real numbers.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with basic algebra: solving two linear equations and finding the area of a triangle. No previous economics is assumed; the depth matches a strong first-year university microeconomics course.

paragraphs: Economics is the study of choice when there is never enough to go round. Time, money and materials can each be used once, so every decision gives something up, and economists learn to count that cost and to see what happens when millions of people make such choices side by side. People study it to understand why prices move, what a tax really does, and how firms and governments behave when their choices affect each other.

The course has twelve lessons in four parts. Choice and cost covers what a decision gives up, who should make what, and how to decide one extra unit at a time. How markets set prices covers demand, supply, what moves them and how strongly buyers react. Welfare and policy covers who gains from a market, then the effects of taxes, price controls and costs that fall on bystanders. Firms and strategy covers costs and profit, monopoly and game theory.
Each lesson explains first and asks afterwards, with short worked numbers rather than long theory.
outcomes: You'll be able to price a choice by what it gives up, and say who should make what.
You'll be able to read demand and supply equations and solve them for the price where a market settles.
You'll be able to work out how a tax, a price control or a shift in buyers' wants changes a market.
You'll be able to find the output and price that maximise a firm's profit.
You'll be able to find the likely outcome of a simple strategic game between two players.
introduction.prerequisites: You should be comfortable with basic algebra, such as solving 100 − 2P = 4P − 20, and with finding the area of a triangle.

modules.title: Choice and cost
modules.description: Opportunity cost, comparative advantage and decisions at the margin.

modules.title: How markets set prices
modules.description: Demand, supply, equilibrium, shifts and elasticity.

modules.title: Welfare and policy
modules.description: Surplus, taxes, price controls and external costs.

modules.title: Firms and strategy
modules.description: Costs, profit, monopoly and game theory.

concepts.title: What it really costs
concepts.summary: Measure opportunity cost along a production possibilities frontier, and see why it usually rises.

concepts.title: Who should make what
concepts.summary: Find comparative advantage from opportunity costs and show that specialisation and trade benefit both sides.

concepts.title: The next unit
concepts.summary: Choose how much of an activity to do by comparing marginal benefit with marginal cost, and ignore sunk costs.

concepts.title: Demand meets supply
concepts.summary: Read linear demand and supply equations and solve them for the equilibrium price and quantity.

concepts.title: When the curves move
concepts.summary: Separate movements along a curve from shifts of it, and solve for the new equilibrium after a shift.

concepts.title: How strongly buyers respond
concepts.summary: Measure price elasticity of demand with the midpoint method and predict what a price change does to revenue.

concepts.title: Who gains from a sale
concepts.summary: Measure consumer and producer surplus as areas on the diagram and see why equilibrium makes their total largest.

concepts.title: What a tax takes
concepts.summary: Work out what a per-unit tax does to prices and revenue. Then measure the surplus it destroys and find who bears it.

concepts.title: Controls and spillovers
concepts.summary: Predict shortages and surpluses from price controls, and correct an external cost with a Pigouvian tax.

concepts.title: Costs and the best output
concepts.summary: Separate fixed, variable, average and marginal cost, and choose output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.

concepts.title: One seller
concepts.summary: Derive a single seller's marginal revenue and use it to find its price and output. Then measure the deadweight loss of monopoly.

concepts.title: Strategic choices
concepts.summary: Find best responses, dominant strategies and Nash equilibria in payoff matrices, and see how repetition supports cooperation.

lessons.title: What it really costs

steps.headline: What a choice really costs

lead.text: Take an afternoon with £20 to spend, where a paperback costs £8 and a bubble tea costs £4. Buy the book and the shop takes £8, which is the price on the label. The same £8 would have bought two teas, though, and once it has gone into the book it can't buy them. So the book has a second price, which is two bubble teas.

Economists call what you give up the opportunity cost of a choice. It is the value of the best alternative you passed over, and the word best matters. Suppose the £8 could also have gone on a magazine or a bus fare. You could only have taken one of them, so the cost of the book is whichever you would really have picked instead, and the others drop out.

Money isn't the only thing that runs out. Time works the same way, since an hour spent on one job is an hour another job can't have. That brings us to a workshop, where the price of one job is counted in the output of another.

lead.text: Now try the idea on a day's budget. Count the cost of the ticket in the thing you could have bought with the same money.

steps.headline: A week's work, priced in chairs

lead.text: Picture a joiner's workshop with one week to use. Workshop B can finish 40 chairs in a week, or 20 tables, if it makes nothing else. Both figures use the whole week, so they are two ways of spending the same time, and that lets us compare them.

Twenty tables take as long as 40 chairs, so one table takes as long as two chairs. Divide the chairs by the tables: 40 ÷ 20 = 2. A table's opportunity cost is 2 chairs, because 2 chairs are what the same time would have built. The rate also works the other way round, and a chair costs half a table.

afterFigure.text: The line in the picture joins the two extremes. The workshop swaps tables for chairs at one steady rate, so every extra table takes the same 2 chairs away. Another workshop with different weekly totals would swap at a different rate, and the next screen gives you one to price.

lead.text: Workshop A has its own week. It can build 60 chairs or 20 tables, and it swaps one for the other at a steady rate. Price a table in chairs, using the method from the last screen.

reveal.text: You just priced a table in chairs: 60 ÷ 20 = 3. That price, the chairs given up for each table, is its opportunity cost.

steps.headline: All the weeks a workshop could choose

lead.text: A workshop doesn't have to put the whole week into one good. Workshop B could give half its week to chairs and half to tables. Half a week of chairs is 20 chairs, and half a week of tables is 10 tables, so 20 chairs and 10 tables is a week it could build. Any other split of the week gives another pair of numbers in the same way.

afterFigure.text: Plot all of those pairs and they join into a line called the production possibilities frontier. It marks the edge of what the workshop can do with its time. On the line, every hour is used. Inside it, a mix such as 10 chairs and 5 tables leaves some hours idle. Beyond it, a mix would need more hours than the week has, so the workshop can't build it.
Each step along the frontier swaps one good for the other, so each step has an opportunity cost, and the next screens read those costs off the line.

cases.label: Workshop B, half a week each
Workshop C, half a week each

lead.text: Workshop A can build 60 chairs or 20 tables in a week at a steady rate. Check where one particular week falls against its frontier.

steps.headline: Pricing a step along a curved frontier

lead.text: So far the swap rate has been the same everywhere along the line. Many real frontiers curve. Take a country that makes food and machines. If it grows no food it can build 100 machines, and if it puts everything into farming it can grow 80 units of food and build none. Between those ends the frontier is a curve, drawn in the picture.

On a curve the price of food depends on where you stand, so we price it one short step at a time. Take the first step, from no food to 20 units. The machines drop from 100 to 90, so 10 machines are given up for 20 more units of food. Each unit of food costs 10 ÷ 20 = 0.5 machines.

afterFigure.text: The rule is the same as before, applied to a step: divide what you give up by what you gain. Next you will price a later step on the same frontier.

steps.headline: A country makes food and machines. Moving from 40 to 60 food, what does each extra unit of food cost?

workedSteps.text: Read the frontier. At 40 food it sits at 70 machines; at 60 food it sits at 40.
Find the machines given up.
Find the food gained.
Share the loss across the gain.

lead.text: Price the next step along the same frontier. An average over the whole frontier would hide how the cost changes from one step to the next.

reveal.text: This step cost 2 machines per unit of food, and the step before it cost 1.5. The price of food is rising.

steps.headline: Why the frontier bows

lead.text: Lay the four steps along the country's frontier side by side. They cost 0.5, 1, 1.5 and 2 machines for each extra unit of food, so the price of food keeps climbing as the country grows more of it. The steps from 20 to 40 and from 40 to 60 give 20 ÷ 20 = 1 and 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5, which fill in the middle.

The reason is that resources aren't equally good at both jobs. The first food comes from fertile land and from workers who did little in the factories, so few machines are lost. Later food has to pull engineers and factory sites onto the farms, and each unit of food then takes more machines with it.

afterFigure.text: A cost that rises like this is called increasing opportunity cost, and it gives the frontier its outward bow. If every resource suited both goods equally, the cost would stay the same at every step and the frontier would be a straight line, like the workshops'.

lead.text: Think about the shape of the country's frontier, a curve that bulges away from the origin.
Not every trade-off bends. Priya splits her study time between essays and problem sets, and each task takes a fixed time, so her trade-off is a straight line.

lessons.orientation: Measure opportunity cost along a production possibilities frontier, and see why it usually rises.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A joiner has one week and one workshop. She can spend the week building chairs or building tables, and a week only has so many hours. Every table she builds uses hours that would have gone into chairs, so a table's real price is the chairs she didn't make.

Your own Saturday works the same way. Money and time can each be spent once, and when you spend them on one thing you give up whatever else they would have bought. Anyone who plans how a business, a household or a whole country uses what it has needs a way of counting that hidden price.

This lesson starts with your own spending and then follows the joiner's week. We'll work out the price of a choice, draw every week she could pick, and watch what happens to the price as she asks more of the workshop.

lessons.title: Who should make what

steps.headline: Counting one job in the other's output

lead.text: The last lesson priced a table in chairs. The same idea works for one person. A potter can make 9 bowls or 3 vases in a day, but not both. Nine bowls and three vases each fill the whole day, so one vase takes as long as three bowls. A vase costs the potter 9 ÷ 3 = 3 bowls.

The price reads the other way too. One bowl takes a third of the time of a vase, so a bowl costs 3 ÷ 9 = a third of a vase. Each good has a price in the other, and the two prices are upside-down versions of each other.
A price like this belongs to one person. A second potter with different daily totals has different prices, and the gap between them is what this lesson is about. First, here is a baker to price.

lead.text: Ana runs a bakery. In a day she can bake loaves or cakes, and the two choices fill the same day. Price a cake in loaves, the way the potter's vase was priced.

steps.headline: Being quicker and being cheaper

lead.text: Now put a second potter next to the first. Jo can make 4 bowls or 2 vases in a day, while the first potter, Mo, makes 9 bowls or 3 vases. Mo is quicker at both jobs. Being able to make more of a good with the same time is called an absolute advantage, and Mo has it in bowls and in vases.

It looks as if Mo should do everything, but look at the prices. A vase costs Mo 3 bowls and costs Jo 4 ÷ 2 = 2 bowls. Jo gives up fewer bowls for each vase, and giving up less is what makes a job cheap. Whoever has the lower opportunity cost of a good has the comparative advantage in it, so Jo has the comparative advantage in vases.

afterFigure.text: Bowls work the other way round. A bowl costs Mo a third of a vase and costs Jo half of one, so Mo has the comparative advantage in bowls. Between two people, each ends up with one of the two jobs, even though one of them is quicker at both.

lead.text: Back to the bakery. Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes a day, and Ben can bake 6 loaves or 4 cakes. Ana is quicker at both jobs, so compare what each baker gives up for one cake.

reveal.text: You compared opportunity costs. A cake costs Ben 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5 loaves and Ana 12 ÷ 6 = 2, so the quicker baker is the dearer one.

steps.headline: Ana bakes 12 loaves or 6 cakes a day; Ben bakes 6 loaves or 4 cakes. Who should bake what?

workedSteps.text: Price a cake in loaves for each baker.
Price a loaf in cakes for each baker.
Give each job to the lower cost: Ben bakes the cakes, Ana bakes the loaves.

steps.headline: Specialising and swapping

lead.text: Knowing who should do which job is only half of it. The gain arrives when each person concentrates on their own job and the two of them swap. Go back to the potters. Suppose Jo makes only vases and Mo makes only bowls, and then Mo pays Jo 2.5 bowls for each vase.

Look at Jo first. Making a vase costs Jo 2 bowls, and Jo is now paid 2.5 bowls for it, so each vase leaves Jo half a bowl ahead. Mo is better off too. Making a vase would cost Mo 3 bowls, and buying one from Jo costs only 2.5, which saves half a bowl a vase.

afterFigure.text: Neither potter has done anything harder than before. They have only moved each job to the person who finds it cheaper, and the saving shows up for both of them.

steps.headline: Which prices suit both

lead.text: The price of 2.5 bowls worked, but other prices could have worked as well. A seller gains from a swap when the price is above what making the good costs them, and a buyer gains when the price is below what making it would cost them. Both are true only between the two opportunity costs.

For the vases, Jo's cost is 2 bowls and Mo's is 3. At a price of 1.5, Jo would lose by selling and would refuse. At a price of 3.5, Mo would do better making the vases without Jo. Anywhere between 2 and 3 helps them both. Close to 2 most of the gain goes to Mo, and close to 3 most of it goes to Jo.

afterFigure.text: The same holds for any pair. Find each side's cost of the good, and every price between the two costs makes both better off.

steps.headline: Ben bakes only cakes and swaps 2 of them with Ana at 1.75 loaves each. Does he come out ahead?

workedSteps.text: Before the swap Ben splits his day, so he makes 2 cakes and 3 loaves.
Now he bakes 4 cakes, keeps 2 and swaps 2 away.
Find the loaves he receives.
Compare with the 3 loaves he used to bake.

lead.text: Ben's cake costs him 1.5 loaves to make and Ana's costs her 2, and they will swap cakes for loaves. Pick the price, in loaves per cake, that leaves both of them better off.
Mira and Tom share a studio and can code web pages or write reports. Start with Tom and find what he gives up for each page he codes.

reveal.text: Tom gives up 4 reports per page and Mira only 2, so Mira has the comparative advantage in pages.

steps.headline: Where the gains come from

lead.text: Every swap so far rested on one fact. The two people give up different amounts for the same good, and the difference opens a range of prices between their costs. Inside that range both sides gain, whichever of them is the quicker worker.

Suppose instead that the costs match. If two bakers each give up the same number of loaves for a cake, a seller gains only above that number and a buyer gains only below it, so no price satisfies both. Being twice as quick at every job changes nothing here, because speed multiplies both of a baker's outputs together and leaves the price of one in terms of the other where it was.

afterFigure.text: So the question to ask of any pair is whether their opportunity costs differ. Speed does not answer it.

lead.text: Cara is twice as productive as Dan at both jobs, which is a large absolute advantage. Check whether that makes a swap worthwhile for them.

reveal.text: Equal costs leave no price that helps both sides. Gains from trade come from differences in opportunity cost, not from differences in productivity.

lessons.orientation: Find comparative advantage from opportunity costs and show that specialisation and trade benefit both sides.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Ana and Ben run bakeries on the same street. In a day Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes, and Ben can bake 6 loaves or 4 cakes. Ana is quicker at both jobs.

That seems to settle things. If Ana can out-bake Ben at everything, she might as well bake everything herself. Yet the two of them would usually do better by splitting the work and swapping. That raises a puzzle: how can the slower baker have anything to offer the quicker one?

The last lesson priced a choice by what it gives up. That same idea answers the puzzle. We'll price each baker's cake in loaves, work out who should bake what, and find the prices at which a swap helps them both.

recap.keyIdea: Comparative advantage belongs to whoever gives up less. Specialise where your cost is lower and trade at a price between the two costs, and both sides gain.

blocks.text: Back at the two bakeries, the puzzle has an answer. Ben's cake costs him 1.5 loaves against Ana's 2, so the slower baker holds the advantage in cakes. A swap at 1.75 loaves left Ben half a loaf ahead, and when two bakers gave up the same amount, there was nothing to swap.

recap.nextHook: Prices in the other good are one kind of cost, and the next lesson looks at how a café decides whether one more hour or one more slice is worth its cost.

lessons.title: The next unit

steps.headline: Deciding one unit at a time

lead.text: Take an ice-cream van where a cone costs £3. On a hot day the first cone is worth £9 to you. The second is worth £6, the third £4 and the fourth only £2, because each cone is less welcome than the one before. A choice about how many to buy is really a string of small choices, one cone at a time.

For each extra cone you ask what it adds and what it costs. What the extra cone adds is its marginal benefit, where marginal simply means one more. What it costs you is its marginal cost, which here is the £3 price. The first cone is worth £9 for £3, so buy it. The second is worth £6 for £3, and the third is worth £4 for £3, so buy both. The fourth is worth £2 for £3, and you stop.

afterFigure.text: The rule is to keep going while the next unit's benefit covers its cost, and to stop when it falls below. For the cones that means three. The rule asks about one extra unit at a time, whatever the total looks like.

diagram.alt: Four bars show what each ice-cream cone is worth to you, £9, £6, £4 and £2, with a dashed line at the £3 price. The first three bars are above the line and the fourth is below it.

lead.text: Use the same rule at a pizza counter. Judge each slice on its own worth against its price, and stop at the first slice that falls short.

steps.headline: When each hour costs more

lead.text: Costs often change from one unit to the next. Take a florist deciding how many late hours to stay open. Each extra hour brings in fewer customers than the one before, and each costs more because the staff are tired and paid extra. The hours bring £50, £40, £25 and £10, and they cost £20, £22, £30 and £35.

Go hour by hour. The first hour brings £50 and costs £20, so open it. The second brings £40 for £22, so open that too. The third brings £25 but costs £30, so it loses money. Stop there, because the fourth hour brings even less against a cost that keeps rising.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the florist never looks at all the hours at once. Each hour is judged against its own cost, and the first hour that falls short ends the search.

lead.text: A café is deciding how many late hours to open. Each extra hour brings in less than the one before and costs more in staff time. Decide hour by hour, as the florist did.

reveal.text: You compared each hour's own benefit with its own cost and stopped where an hour stopped paying. The best choice sits where marginal benefit meets marginal cost.

steps.headline: Adding up what the hours earn

lead.text: Once you know which hours to open, you can say how much the choice gains. An hour's net benefit is its benefit minus its cost. For the florist the first hour nets £50 − £20 = £30 and the second nets £40 − £22 = £18. The third nets £25 − £30 = −£5, a loss, which is why it stays closed.

The total net benefit of a plan is the sum of the net benefits of the hours in it. Opening two hours gives £30 + £18 = £48. Opening a third as well would give £48 − £5 = £43, which is less. The same happens with any hour that nets a loss, so the best plan includes every hour with a positive net benefit and no others.

diagram.alt: Bars for the florist's late hours. One view shows each hour's net benefit: £30, £18, minus £5 and minus £25. The other shows the total net benefit after each hour: £30, £48, £43 and £18.
diagram.caption: Use the buttons to see each hour, then the running total. The third hour nets a loss, so adding it lowers the total.

steps.headline: A bookshop can open late for up to four hours at £30 an hour. How many hours should it open, and what does it gain?

workedSteps.text: The four hours bring £80, £60, £40 and £20. Find each hour's net gain, which is its benefit minus its cost.
Open every hour whose net gain is positive: the first three.
Add their gains.

steps.headline: The café opens its first three late hours. What total net benefit does it gain?

workedSteps.text: Hour 1: benefit £90, cost £30.
Hour 2: benefit £70, cost £35. Find its net benefit.
Hour 3: benefit £55, cost £45.
Add the three net benefits.

steps.headline: Costs that are already paid

lead.text: Some costs are paid already, whatever you decide next. Suppose you bought a non-refundable £25 ticket for a concert, and on the night you feel ill. The £25 has gone either way. Stay home and you've lost it, and go and you've lost it too.

A cost like that is called a sunk cost. Because it is the same under every option, it can't tip a choice between them. The sensible comparison is between what going adds and what it costs from here on, which means an evening of music while ill against an evening in bed. The £25 appears on neither side.

afterFigure.text: The same holds for a business. A café that paid a licence last month has paid it whether or not it opens a fourth hour tonight, so the licence plays no part in tonight's decision. Only the extra hour's own benefit and cost matter, which is the rule we have been using all along.

diagram.alt: Two columns, stay home and go to the concert. Each holds the same already-paid £25 ticket, and below it the real difference: an evening in bed or an evening of music while ill.
diagram.caption: The £25 sits in both columns, so it can't decide between them.

lead.text: A café paid its licence fee last month and can't get it back. Apply the test from the last screen to the fee.
Staffing now gets dearer, so every hour costs £20 more than before. Decide again, hour by hour.

reveal.text: Dearer hours moved the stopping point from the third hour to the second. When marginal cost rises, the best amount falls.

steps.headline: Why an average can mislead

lead.text: A tempting shortcut is to judge an hour by the average of the hours before it. The florist's first three hours bring £50, £40 and £25, which is £115 in total and an average of about £38 an hour. Set that against the third hour's £30 cost and it looks comfortably worth opening.

The average hides what the third hour itself did. The first two hours bring £90, and adding the third lifts the total from £90 to £115. So the third hour's marginal benefit is £115 − £90 = £25, which is below its £30 cost. The average was £38, yet the hour that actually decided things earned £25.

afterFigure.text: Marginal means the change in the total from one more unit, so you find it by subtracting one total from the next. Judge the extra hour by that figure and by its own cost, since the hours already open stay open either way.

diagram.alt: A bar of the florist's first three hours, £50, £40 and £25, totalling £115. The second view picks out the third hour, £25, against its £30 cost.
diagram.caption: The average of £38 hides that the third hour adds only £25. Use the buttons to move from the average to the hour itself.

reveal.text: The average includes hours that are being opened anyway. Only the extra hour's own benefit and cost decide the extra hour.

lessons.orientation: Choose how much of an activity to do by comparing marginal benefit with marginal cost, and ignore sunk costs.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: You are at a pizza counter, and a slice costs £4. The first slice is wonderful. The second is good but a little less so, and by the fifth you could take it or leave it. Every extra slice is worth a bit less to you than the one before, while the price on the counter stays the same.

Most real choices come in units like this: another slice, another hour of work, another batch from the oven. We seldom choose between everything and nothing. The question is usually whether to have one more.
This lesson gives you a way of settling that question. We'll weigh one more unit at a time, follow a florist and a café as they decide how late to stay open, and see why some costs should be ignored.

intro.promise: By the end you'll decide how much to do by comparing the next unit's benefit with its cost, and ignore costs already paid.

recap.keyIdea: Decide one extra unit at a time. Keep going while the next unit's benefit covers its cost, and ignore costs already paid.

blocks.text: Back at the counter, the choice of how many has become a string of small ones. You bought four slices and opened three late hours. When costs rose the café opened only two, and the fourth hour would have lost £10 even though the average looked good.

recap.nextHook: You can now say how much one more unit is worth to one buyer, and the next lesson asks how a whole street of buyers and sellers settles on a price.

lessons.title: Demand meets supply

steps.headline: How buyers respond to price

lead.text: Start with the buyers. At a lolly stall in summer, the lower the price the more lollies people buy. At £2 the stall sells plenty, and at £8 only the keenest customers are left. The same pattern holds for nearly every good, and it is called the law of demand: when the price rises, the amount people want to buy falls, provided nothing else changes.

The amount buyers plan to buy at a given price is called the quantity demanded. It describes a plan and not a sale that has happened. Each price has its own quantity demanded, and the whole list, from low prices to high, is what economists call demand.

afterFigure.text: Because the plan changes steadily with the price, it can be written as a rule. The next screens turn that rule into an equation.

steps.headline: Writing demand as an equation

lead.text: Suppose the lolly stall finds that each £1 on the price loses it 5 lollies a day, and that at a price of £0 it could give away 60. Then the quantity demanded, written Qd, follows the rule Qd = 60 − 5P, where P is the price in pounds. At £4 the stall sells 60 − 5 × 4 = 40 lollies. At £8 it sells 60 − 5 × 8 = 20.

Each number in the rule means something. The 60 is the quantity demanded when the price is zero. The 5 is the number of lollies that each £1 of price takes away, so a bigger number there means buyers react more strongly to a change in price. To use the rule, put a price in and it hands back the quantity.

diagram.caption: A bigger number in front of P means buyers react more strongly to price. Use the buttons to compare 5 with 10.

lead.text: The coffee stall's demand is Qd = 100 − 2P, where P is the price in pounds and Q is cups a day. Put a price in and the equation gives the cups buyers plan to take.

reveal.text: You turned a price into a quantity, which is what the demand equation does. At £15 buyers plan 70 cups, and at £30 they would plan only 40.

steps.headline: How sellers respond to price

lead.text: Sellers react the other way round. A higher price makes it worth stocking more, hiring extra help and opening longer, so the amount sellers plan to offer rises with the price. This is the supply side of the market, and the amount sellers plan to offer at a given price is the quantity supplied, written Qs.

Suppose the sellers of lollies offer 5 lollies a day for every £1 of price, so Qs = 5P. At £4 they offer 20 lollies and at £8 they offer 40. Some supply rules start below zero, as in Qs = 4P − 20. That means sellers offer nothing at a low price, because the price doesn't cover what the good costs them to make.

afterFigure.text: Now there is a rule for each side. Buyers want less as the price climbs while sellers offer more, so the rules pull in opposite directions and must cross somewhere.

steps.headline: Where buyers and sellers agree

lead.text: Put the lolly stall's two rules side by side, Qd = 60 − 5P and Qs = 5P. At £4, buyers want 60 − 5 × 4 = 40 lollies and sellers offer 5 × 4 = 20. Buyers want a larger quantity than sellers offer, and that excess is called a shortage. Shoppers compete for the lollies that are there, and sellers notice that they could ask for more.

At £8 the picture reverses. Buyers want 60 − 5 × 8 = 20 and sellers offer 40, so 20 lollies are left over, an excess called a surplus. Sellers stuck with stock cut their price. A shortage pushes the price up and a surplus pushes it down, and each move closes the gap.

afterFigure.text: The price stops moving where the gap is zero. At £6, buyers want 60 − 5 × 6 = 30 and sellers offer 5 × 6 = 30. That price is the equilibrium price, and the 30 lollies that change hands are the equilibrium quantity. At equilibrium every plan can be carried out: each lolly offered finds a buyer, and nobody willing to pay goes without.

lead.text: Think about the lolly stall at £6, where the two rules gave the same quantity.

steps.headline: Finding the price from the equations

lead.text: The picture finds equilibrium by trying prices. The equations let us skip the trying. At equilibrium the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied, so we set the two rules equal and solve for the price.

For the lolly stall that gives 60 − 5P = 5P. Add 5P to both sides to collect the P terms, which gives 60 = 10P. Divide both sides by 10 and P = 6. To find the quantity, put the price into either rule: 60 − 5 × 6 = 30, and 5 × 6 = 30 agrees. Any pair of rules is solved the same way, by setting them equal, collecting the P terms and dividing.

afterFigure.text: It is worth checking at the end that both rules give the same quantity at your price. If they don't, an arithmetic slip has crept in.

lead.text: A café fixes its coffee price at £25, above the price where plans match. See what that does to the cups offered and the cups people want.

reveal.text: At £25 sellers offer 80 cups and buyers want only 50, a surplus of 30. Unsold stock pushes sellers to cut the price. At £15 the reverse holds, a shortage of 30.

blocks.text: A coffee stall on a busy street has been experimenting with its price. It has found that every £1 it adds loses it the same number of customers, which makes its sales easy to predict. Meanwhile the café down the road sells coffee too, and it is trying prices of its own.

Nobody tells the street what coffee should cost, and yet prices on a street like this settle down. Cups don't pile up unsold for long, and shoppers seldom find every stall out of coffee. Something brings what buyers want and what sellers offer into line.
This lesson shows what that something is. We'll describe buyers with one rule and sellers with another, then find the price at which the two agree.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read demand and supply equations and solve them for the price where a market settles.

recap.keyIdea: Equilibrium is the price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied. Set the equations equal, solve for the price, then substitute it back to find the quantity.

blocks.text: Back on the street, the settling price now has an explanation. You turned a price into cups for the buyers' rule and for the sellers' rule, then solved for £20 and 60 cups in the coffee market. A price stuck at £25 left 30 cups unsold.

recap.nextHook: The market now has a settling price, and the next lesson asks what happens to it when a fad for coffee arrives and buyers want more at every price.

lessons.title: When the curves move

steps.headline: Sliding along a curve and moving it

lead.text: Look again at the lolly stall's demand rule, Qd = 60 − 5P. Price sits inside it. If the stall raises its price from £4 to £6, the quantity demanded falls from 40 to 30. Buyers haven't changed their minds about lollies. They are reacting to the price, and on a graph that is a slide along the same demand curve, called a movement along the curve.

Now suppose a heatwave arrives. At every price people want 10 more lollies than before, so the rule becomes Qd = 70 − 5P. At £4 the quantity demanded is now 50 instead of 40, although the price hasn't changed. The whole curve has moved to the right, and that is called a shift.

afterFigure.text: So the test is short. If the cause is a change in the good's own price, you slide along the curve. If the cause is anything else, the curve itself moves. The word demand names the whole curve, and quantity demanded names one point on it.

lead.text: Use the test from the last screen on the coffee market.

steps.headline: What shifts demand and supply

lead.text: A shift needs a cause other than the good's own price. The clearest cause on the demand side is buyers' income. When incomes rise people buy more of most things, so demand shifts right. A fall in incomes shifts it left. Tastes move demand too, and the heatwave was a change in taste for cold lollies. Expectations about future prices also move it, as do the prices of related goods.

Related goods come in pairs that behave differently. Substitutes are goods that can replace each other, such as tea and coffee. If the price of tea goes up, some tea drinkers switch to coffee, and the demand for coffee shifts right even though coffee's own price hasn't moved.

afterFigure.text: Supply shifts for its own reasons. A cheaper ingredient lets sellers offer more at every price, which shifts supply right. A dearer ingredient shifts it left. Better technology also moves supply to the right, as does a rise in the number of sellers.

diagram.alt: Two lists of causes. For the demand curve: rising incomes, falling incomes, a dearer substitute and a growing taste each point left or right. For the supply curve: a cheaper or dearer ingredient, better technology and more sellers.
diagram.caption: Each cause moves its curve one way. Use the buttons to move between demand and supply.

lead.text: Tea and coffee can replace each other. Work out what a change in one does to the other.

steps.headline: Finding the new price after a shift

lead.text: A shift breaks the old balance, so the price has to move to find a new one. The method is to write the new equation for the curve that moved and leave the other curve alone. Then solve for equilibrium as before.

Take the heatwave. Demand becomes Qd = 70 − 5P and supply stays Qs = 5P. At the old price of £6, buyers now want 70 − 30 = 40 lollies and sellers still offer 30, a shortage of 10. Set the new rule equal to supply: 70 − 5P = 5P, so 70 = 10P and P = 7. The quantity is 5 × 7 = 35.

afterFigure.text: Both the price and the quantity rose, from £6 and 30 to £7 and 35. A rightward shift of demand along an unchanged supply curve does that. The next questions run the same steps on the coffee market.

lead.text: The coffee fad adds to demand at every price. Check what it does at the old price first.

steps.headline: Incomes fall and buyers want 30 fewer cups at every price. Find the new equilibrium for Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20.

workedSteps.text: Demand shifts left by 30 cups at every price.
Supply is untouched. Set the new demand equal to it.
Collect terms.
Solve for the price, then the quantity.

steps.headline: Incomes rise and buyers want 30 more cups at every price. Find the new equilibrium.

workedSteps.text: Demand shifts right.
Set it equal to the unchanged supply.
Solve for the price.
Find the quantity.

steps.headline: When supply moves instead

lead.text: A change on the sellers' side moves the supply curve, and the same steps work. Suppose the price of sugar rises, so lolly makers offer 10 fewer lollies at every price. The supply rule Qs = 5P becomes Qs = 5P − 10, and demand is untouched at Qd = 60 − 5P.

Set them equal: 60 − 5P = 5P − 10, so 70 = 10P and P = 7. The quantity is 60 − 35 = 25. The heatwave also took the price to £7, but there the quantity rose to 35. Here it fell to 25, because supply moved left.

afterFigure.text: The pattern is worth remembering. A shift in demand moves price and quantity in the same direction, and a shift in supply moves them in opposite directions. That holds whichever way the curve moves.

lead.text: Now a frost hits the harvest. A cause on the supply side moves the supply curve, and demand stays where it was.

reveal.text: Supply shifted left, so the price rose from £20 to £24 and the quantity fell from 60 to 52. You solved it the same way as a demand shift.

steps.headline: When both curves move

lead.text: Sometimes demand and supply move at once. Back at the lolly stall, suppose the heatwave raises demand by 10 at every price and a new lolly maker raises supply by 20 at every price. The rules are Qd = 70 − 5P and Qs = 5P + 20.

Setting them equal gives 70 − 5P = 5P + 20, so 50 = 10P and P = 5. The quantity is 70 − 25 = 45. The price fell from £6 to £5 and the quantity rose from 30 to 45. Quantity rose because both shifts push it up. The price fell because supply moved further than demand.

afterFigure.text: The size of each shift decides which way the price goes, so the new equations have to be written out and solved. A guess from the directions alone is not enough.

lead.text: Now demand and supply each grow by the same number of cups at every price. Write both new equations and solve them together.

reveal.text: The quantity rose from 60 to 90 and the price stayed at £20, because the two shifts were equal. Equal shifts to the right raise the quantity and leave the price alone.

lessons.orientation: Separate movements along a curve from shifts of it, and solve for the new equilibrium after a shift.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The coffee market from the last lesson has settled at £20 and 60 cups a day. Then a fad for coffee arrives. People who never drank it want a cup, and at the old price the stalls find a queue forming.

Something has to change. The price may rise, the stalls may sell out, or both may happen, and which it is depends on what kind of change has hit the market. A rise in the price of coffee itself works differently from a fad, a frost that damages the crop or a new factory, and mixing the two up gives wrong answers.
This lesson sorts out the difference. We'll learn to tell a slide along a curve from a move of the whole curve, and then work out the new price and quantity after each kind of change.

intro.promise: By the end you'll tell a movement along a curve from a shift of it, and solve for the new equilibrium.

recap.keyIdea: A change in the good's own price moves you along a curve. Anything else shifts the curve, and you find the new equilibrium by solving again with the new equation.

blocks.text: Back at the coffee market, the fad now has a result. You found a shortage of 12 cups at the old price, then £15 when incomes fell and £25 when they rose. A frost lifted the price to £24, and shifting both curves by the same amount left it at £20.

recap.nextHook: A change in price moves the quantity, and the next lesson asks how far it moves, which depends on how strongly buyers react.

lessons.title: How strongly buyers respond

steps.headline: What a price cut does to takings

lead.text: The money a seller takes in is called revenue, and it is the price multiplied by the number sold. A baker who sells 85 loaves a day at £3 has revenue of £3 × 85 = £255.

Now the baker drops the price to £2 and sales rise to 115 loaves. Buyers have clearly responded, since 30 more loaves go out each day. Yet revenue is now £2 × 115 = £230, which is £25 less than before.

afterFigure.text: A price cut shrinks one half of the sum and grows the other, so more sales do not guarantee more money. Which half wins depends on how far sales climb compared with how far the price fell.
That comparison is what the owners of both stalls need. Knowing that buyers respond is not enough, because the question is how strongly they respond. The next two screens turn that into a number.

lead.text: The snack stall cuts its price and the owner counts the day's takings. Work out whether the cut paid.

steps.headline: Putting each change on the same footing

lead.text: A change of 30 loaves and a change of £1 cannot be compared directly, because loaves and pounds are different units. Turning each into a percentage puts them on the same footing.

That brings a small trap. The baker's price fell from £3 to £2, which is a fall of a third when measured from £3. If it rose back from £2 to £3, that is a rise of a half when measured from £2. The same £1 gap gives two different percentages depending on where you start.

afterFigure.text: The fix is to measure each change against the average of the two values. For the baker's price the average of £3 and £2 is £2.50, so the £1 change is £1 ÷ £2.50 = 40%. For the loaves the average of 85 and 115 is 100, so the change of 30 is 30%. Going from £3 to £2 or from £2 to £3 now gives the same percentage.
This way of measuring is called the midpoint method. It gives one answer for a pair of prices whichever way the price moved, which is why it is used whenever two percentages are to be compared.

steps.headline: A single number for how buyers react

lead.text: Both changes are now percentages, so one can be divided by the other. The baker's quantity changed by 30% and the price by 40%, so the ratio is 30% ÷ 40% = 0.75. This ratio is the price elasticity of demand. Price and quantity move in opposite directions, so the raw ratio is negative. We quote its size and leave the sign off.

afterFigure.text: The dividing line is 1. Above 1, quantity moved by a bigger percentage than price did, and demand is called elastic. Below 1, quantity moved by a smaller percentage and demand is called inelastic. The baker's 0.75 is inelastic.

The figure shows the two stalls from the start of the lesson. The snack stall's buyers react strongly, with an elasticity of about 1.8, so its demand is elastic. The pharmacy's buyers hardly react at all, with an elasticity of about 0.15, so its demand is inelastic. Whether a price change fills or drains the till depends on which side of 1 the elasticity falls.

lead.text: A seller raises a price by 10% and sees quantity demanded fall by 30%. Divide the two percentages and compare the result with 1.

steps.headline: A gym's price rises from £4 to £6 a visit and visits fall from 130 to 70 a day. What is the elasticity of demand?

workedSteps.text: Quantity change as a share of the average quantity.
Price change as a share of the average price.
Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.
Above 1, so demand is elastic.

steps.headline: A bus pass falls from £6 to £4 and passes sold rise from 95 to 105. What is the elasticity of demand?

workedSteps.text: The average quantity is 100 and the quantity changes by 10.
The average price is £5 and the price changes by £2.
Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.

lead.text: Same method, a different market. Find the average of each pair first, then divide the two percentage changes.

reveal.text: Elasticity of 3 is well above 1: demand for tickets is elastic, so buyers respond more than in proportion.

steps.headline: Elasticity and takings

lead.text: Elasticity tells you what a price change does to revenue. Suppose a seller cuts the price by 10%. If demand is elastic, quantity rises by more than 10%, so the gain in sales outweighs the lost price and revenue goes up. If demand is inelastic, quantity rises by less than 10%, so the price cut costs more than the extra sales bring in and revenue goes down. At an elasticity of exactly 1 the two cancel and revenue stays put.
A price rise is the mirror image. With inelastic demand, quantity falls by less than the price rose, so the seller takes in more.

afterFigure.text: The two stalls fit the rule. The snack stall's elasticity of about 1.8 means its £1 cut brought more money in, as the count showed. The baker's 0.75 means the cut to £2 lost money, as the £25 shortfall showed. The same logic explains why a seller of a necessity, such as medicine, can raise the price and still see takings grow.

lead.text: The concert tickets had an elasticity of 3. Work out what that price cut did to the money taken at the box office.

reveal.text: Revenue rose from 11 × 35 = £385 to 9 × 65 = £585, as the rule says for elastic demand.

steps.headline: One demand line, many elasticities

lead.text: So far each market has had a single elasticity, but a straight demand line does not. Take a museum whose demand is Qd = 200 − 10P. When the entry price falls from £15 to £13, visits rise from 50 to 70. That is 20 on an average of 60, about 33%, against a price change of 2 on an average of 14, about 14%. The elasticity is about 2.3, so demand is elastic and revenue grows from £750 to £910.

afterFigure.text: Lower down the same line the picture reverses. A cut from £6 to £4 lifts visits from 140 to 160, which is only about 13% on an average of 150, while the price fell by 40%. The elasticity is about 0.33, so demand is inelastic and revenue drops from £840 to £640.

The line is straight, so the slope never changes. The percentages do. Near the top of the line a £2 cut is a small share of a high price, while 20 extra visits are a large share of a small quantity. Near the bottom it is the other way round. So the elasticity falls steadily as the price falls, and somewhere between the two stretches it must pass through 1.

lead.text: The elasticity passes through 1 somewhere between those two stretches. Test a price cut that straddles the middle of the museum's demand line.

reveal.text: Revenue is £990 at both prices, so elasticity here is exactly 1. On a straight line demand is elastic at high prices and inelastic at low ones, and revenue peaks where it equals 1.

lessons.orientation: Measure price elasticity of demand with the midpoint method and predict what a price change does to revenue.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A snack stall sells 60 snacks a day at £5 each. Across the road, a pharmacy sells 60 packs of painkillers a day, also at £5 a pack. Each owner is thinking of cutting the price by £1, and each wants to know whether the till will be fuller after closing time.

The last lesson showed that a lower price moves buyers along the demand curve to a larger quantity. It did not say how much larger, and that decides the matter. People queueing for snacks might jump at a cheaper one. Someone with a headache needs one pack and buys one pack, whatever the price.

The same £1 cut could fill one till and drain the other. To tell which, we need a number for how strongly buyers react to a change in price. This lesson builds that number from two ordinary percentages, shows how to read it, and uses it to say what a price change does to the money coming in.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure how strongly buyers respond to price, and say what a price change does to revenue.

recap.keyIdea: Elasticity is the percentage change in quantity over the percentage change in price, taken at the midpoint. Elastic demand means a price cut raises revenue; inelastic demand means it lowers it.

blocks.text: Back at the two stalls, the snack stall's elasticity of about 1.8 explains why its cut paid, and the baker's 0.75 explains why a cut lost money. Along the way you measured 1.5 for gym visits, 0.25 for bus passes and 3 for concert tickets. At the museum, revenue stayed at £990 where elasticity was exactly 1.

recap.nextHook: Buyers react to price because every buyer has a limit on what a thing is worth to them. The next lesson measures the gap between that limit and the price actually paid.

lessons.title: Who gains from a sale

steps.headline: What a ticket is worth to you

lead.text: Every buyer has a highest price they would pay for a thing, and a price above it sends them home empty-handed. That limit is their willingness to pay. It belongs to the buyer and not to the shop. Mia, who has been saving for headphones, might be willing to pay up to £50 for a pair, while her brother, who owns three pairs already, would pay no more than £20.

Suppose the headphones cost £40. Mia buys them. She hands over £40 for something she values at £50, so she is £10 better off than if the price had been her limit. That gap between her willingness to pay and the price she paid is called consumer surplus. Her brother does not buy, and his consumer surplus is zero.

The price is the same for both of them, yet each gets a different surplus because each has a different limit. A shop cannot see those limits, and a market with many buyers holds a whole range of them. Counting the surplus of a group means adding up one gap for each buyer who buys.
Back to the three friends. Tickets cost £22, and a friend buys only if their limit reaches the price. Add up the gaps for those who buy.

steps.headline: The seller's side of the bargain

lead.text: Sellers have a limit too, pointing the other way. The lowest price a seller will accept for a unit is usually what it costs them to supply it, because selling below cost loses money. A baker whose flour, oven time and labour cost £2 a loaf will take any price from £2 upwards.

If she sells a loaf at £3.50, she keeps £1.50 more than she needed to make the sale. That gap between the price received and the lowest price she would accept is her producer surplus. A second baker with a cheaper oven can make a loaf for £1. At the same £3.50 he keeps £2.50, so the lower a seller's cost, the more the market price gives them.
Buyers' surplus sits above the price they pay, and sellers' surplus sits below the price they receive. One picture holds both: the supply and demand diagram. The next screen reads the surplus off it.

steps.headline: Adding up the gaps on the diagram

lead.text: Take the lolly stall from the earlier lessons, where demand is Qd = 60 − 5P and supply is Qs = 5P. The market price is £6 and 30 lollies sell each day. The height of the demand curve at each quantity is the willingness to pay of the buyer of that lolly, so the first buyers would pay almost £12 and the 30th would pay exactly £6.

Each buyer's surplus is the gap between that height and the price, and standing the gaps side by side fills a triangle. It lies below the demand curve and above the price line, out to the 30 lollies sold.

afterFigure.text: The triangle's base is the quantity sold, 30. Its height runs from the price of £6 up to where the demand curve reaches zero. Setting 60 − 5P = 0 gives £12, so the height is 12 − 6 = 6. The area of a triangle is half of base times height, so consumer surplus is ½ × 30 × 6 = £90.

Producer surplus is the matching triangle below the price and above the supply curve. This supply curve starts at £0, so its height is 6 − 0 = 6 and its area is also ½ × 30 × 6 = £90. The second case in the figure shows what dearer sugar does to both triangles.

lead.text: Use the triangles from the last screen to say which area belongs to buyers.

steps.headline: Bagels: Qd = 90 − 3P and Qs = 2P − 10. Find consumer surplus.

workedSteps.text: Find the equilibrium price and quantity.
Find the price at which demand reaches zero.
The base is the quantity sold; the height is the gap between that price and the market price.
Take half of base times height.

steps.headline: Coffee sells 60 cups at £20, with Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20. Find both surpluses.

workedSteps.text: Demand reaches zero at £50, so the buyers' height is the gap above the price.
Half of base times height gives consumer surplus.
Supply starts at £5, so the sellers' height is the gap below the price.
Half of base times height gives producer surplus.

lead.text: A different market, the same triangle. Find the market price first.

reveal.text: Same moves: equilibrium, the price where demand reaches zero, then half of base times height.

steps.headline: Why the market's own quantity is the best one

lead.text: Consumer surplus and producer surplus are the two shares of the gain from trade. Added together they make total surplus, the whole gain a market produces. How the total is split depends on the price. How large it is depends on which trades take place.

A trade adds to the total whenever the buyer's willingness to pay is above the seller's cost. A lolly that a buyer values at £9 and that costs £4 to make creates £5 of value, and the price only decides how that £5 is shared. A trade where the cost is above the value would use up more than it creates.

afterFigure.text: Equilibrium is the quantity where the last trade is only just worth making. Up to it, every lolly has a buyer who values it above its cost, so every one of those trades happens. Beyond it, the 31st lolly would cost sellers about £6.20 to make and be worth only £5.80 to the next buyer. That trade would shrink the total, and the market does not make it.
So a market left alone trades every worthwhile unit and no other. In the lolly market that leaves total surplus of £90 + £90 = £180, the largest it can be.

lead.text: Apply the same test to a single cup. The buyer's value and the maker's cost are both given.

steps.headline: When trades are blocked

lead.text: Equilibrium is the best the market can do, so anything that stops worthwhile trades makes the total smaller. Suppose a rule caps lolly sales at 20 a day, below the 30 the market would make. The buyers of the 21st to 30th lollies, who each value a lolly above its cost, now go without.

Look at the 20th lolly. Its buyer would pay £8 and its seller could supply it for £4, so £4 of gain is available there. The gap shrinks steadily to nothing at the 30th lolly, so the gains that are lost form a triangle.

afterFigure.text: The base is the 10 lollies that no longer sell (30 − 20) and the height is the £4 gap at the cap, so the area is ½ × 10 × 4 = £20. Total surplus falls from £180 to £160. No buyer or seller receives the missing £20, because the trades that would have created it do not happen.

lead.text: Now a rule caps coffee sales below the free-market quantity. The cups that can no longer be sold are the ones to look at.

reveal.text: The lost value is the triangle of base 20 and height 15: £150 of surplus that nobody gets.

lessons.orientation: Measure consumer and producer surplus as areas on the diagram and see why equilibrium makes their total largest.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Three friends want to see the same band. Asha would pay up to £30 for a ticket, Ben up to £25 and Cara up to £20. None of them says so out loud, but each has a number in mind, and the buyers in the last lesson reacted to price because of numbers like these.

Tickets go on sale at one fixed price. A friend buys if the price is at or below their number, and stays at home if it is above. A friend who pays less than their number gets a bargain, and the size of that bargain is something real that can be counted.

This lesson counts it, first for buyers and then for sellers. It adds the counts up as areas on the supply and demand diagram and uses them to show why a market left alone makes the total gain as large as it can be.

intro.promise: By the end you'll measure who gains from a sale as areas on the diagram, and show why equilibrium makes the total largest.

recap.keyIdea: Consumer surplus is the gap between what buyers would pay and the price. Producer surplus is the gap between the price and what sellers would accept. Equilibrium makes their total as large as possible.

blocks.text: Back with the three friends, the tickets left £11 of surplus with the two who bought. In the coffee market you found £900 of consumer surplus and £450 of producer surplus, and a cap at 40 cups wasted £150 of it.

recap.nextHook: A blocked trade destroys surplus, and a tax stops some trades too. The next lesson follows a tax through the coffee market to see who pays it and what it costs.

lessons.title: What a tax takes

steps.headline: Two prices where there was one

lead.text: Before any tax, a cup of coffee has one price. Buyers pay it and sellers keep it. A per-unit tax collected from sellers is a fixed sum on every cup sold, and it splits that one price in two. The price buyers pay is what they hand over at the till. The price sellers keep is what is left after they pass the tax to the government.

Take an ice-cream van that sells cones at £5 with no tax. A £2 tax on every cone arrives. Suppose cones now sell at £6. Buyers pay £6, and the van keeps £6 − £2 = £4. The gap between the two prices is always exactly the tax, and it is called the tax wedge.

afterFigure.text: Notice that the cone price rose by £1 and the van's take fell by £1, so each side carries half of the tax. Nothing forces an even split. How the £2 is divided depends on how the market settles, and the next two screens find out how to work that out. First, the wedge has a consequence that is easy to miss: sellers decide how many cones to offer by what they keep, not by what buyers pay.

lead.text: Back to the coffee market, where cups sold for £10 before the £6 tax. Use the wedge to find what sellers keep after it.

steps.headline: Finding the price after a tax

lead.text: Buyers decide how many cups to buy from the price they pay, so the demand equation stays as it is. Sellers decide how many to offer from the price they keep, which is the buyers' price minus the tax. So the supply equation changes: wherever it has P, write P minus the tax.

Try it on the lolly stall, where demand is Qd = 60 − 5P and supply is Qs = 5P. A £2 tax turns supply into Qs = 5(P − 2) = 5P − 10. Setting that equal to demand gives 60 − 5P = 5P − 10, so 70 = 10P and P = 7. Buyers pay £7, up from £6, and sellers keep 7 − 2 = £5, down from £6.

afterFigure.text: The quantity is found by putting £7 into demand: 60 − 35 = 25 lollies, down from 30. Check the sellers' side too: at the £5 they keep, supply is 5 × 5 = 25, which matches. The tax has pushed buyers and sellers apart by £2 and trade has shrunk by 5 lollies. The second case in the figure shows a £4 tax, which opens a wider wedge and shrinks trade further.

steps.headline: Demand is Qd = 60 − 2P and supply is Qs = 2P − 20. A £4 tax is collected from sellers. Find the buyers' price, the quantity and the revenue.

workedSteps.text: Sellers keep P − 4, so supply in terms of the buyers' price changes.
Set it equal to demand.
Collect terms and solve.
Find the quantity, then the revenue.

lead.text: Now the coffee market. Sellers hand over £6 on every cup, so their supply depends on the buyers' price minus 6. Replace P in the supply equation and solve.

reveal.text: You found that buyers pay £24 and sellers keep £18. The £6 tax is shared: £4 to buyers and £2 to sellers.

steps.headline: What the government collects

lead.text: The tax raises money only on the units that still sell. Each unit sold brings in the full tax, so revenue is the tax per unit times the number of units traded after the tax. In the lolly market the £2 tax is collected on 25 lollies, so the government receives 2 × 25 = £50 a day.
That is less than the 2 × 30 = £60 you might expect from the old quantity. The five lollies that no longer sell pay no tax, and they are the first sign of a cost the tax brings with it.

afterFigure.text: A bigger tax does not simply bring in more. Raise the lolly tax to £4 and the quantity falls to 20, so revenue is 4 × 20 = £80. The rate doubled and the revenue rose by only a little more than half, because trade shrank as the tax grew. The next screen turns to the trades that disappeared.

steps.headline: The trades the tax stops

lead.text: The five lost lollies were all worth making. Look at the 25th: a buyer would pay £7 for it, and a seller could supply it for £5. That £2 gap is the tax itself, so the tax wedge sits exactly where trade is stopped. At the 30th lolly, the old quantity, the buyer's value and the seller's cost were equal and there was nothing to lose.

Between the 25th and 30th the gaps shrink steadily from £2 to nothing. The gains that vanish form a triangle, like the one lost to the cap in the last lesson. Its base is the 5 lollies no longer traded and its height is the £2 tax. Its area is ½ × 2 × 5 = £5.

afterFigure.text: This lost surplus is called deadweight loss. Nobody gets it. The government does not collect it and neither buyers nor sellers keep it, since the trades that would have created it do not happen. The rule is the same for any straight-line market: deadweight loss is half of the tax times the fall in quantity.

lead.text: Apply the last screen's idea to coffee. A tax stops some cups from being sold, and the question is which cups make up the loss.

steps.headline: With the £6 tax, coffee sales fall from 60 to 52 cups a day. Find the revenue and the deadweight loss.

workedSteps.text: Tax per cup times the cups still sold gives the revenue.
Cups no longer sold.
Half of the tax times that fall gives the deadweight loss.

steps.headline: Who really pays

lead.text: In the coffee market the £6 tax leaves buyers paying £24 and sellers keeping £18. Before the tax the price was £20, so buyers pay £4 more and sellers keep £2 less. The tax is shared, but not equally.

The split follows how strongly each side reacts. Coffee demand falls by 2 cups for every £1 on the price, while supply rises by 4 cups for every £1 sellers keep. Sellers react more strongly, so they find it easier to cut back and bear less of the tax. Buyers react less, so they stay and pay more. It is the same idea as elasticity: the side that has less room to walk away carries more of the burden.

afterFigure.text: The second case in the figure shows buyers who react very little, with demand falling by 1 cup for every £1. The price they pay rises by £4.50 of the £6, and sellers lose only £1.50. Whichever side the law names as the payer, the split is decided by how readily each side can leave the market.

lead.text: Now gym passes, where buyers are more price-sensitive than sellers. The same £6 tax is collected from sellers. Compare what happens to the price buyers pay.

reveal.text: Buyers' price rises from £25 to £27: they bear £2 of the £6, against £4 in the coffee market. The side that can more easily walk away bears less.

lessons.orientation: Work out what a per-unit tax does to prices and revenue. Then measure the surplus it destroys and find who bears it.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The government announces a tax of £6 on every cup of coffee, collected from the sellers. It sounds simple. Sellers hand over £6 a cup, so the price goes up by £6 and the customers cover the bill.

The last two lessons suggest it will not work out so neatly. A dearer cup means buyers buy fewer cups, and every cup that goes unbought is a trade that would have left both sides better off. If sellers raise the price by the full £6 they lose customers, so they may choose to absorb part of the tax themselves.

This lesson follows the £6 tax through the coffee market. It finds the new price and quantity, works out who ends up paying, counts what the government collects and measures the surplus the tax destroys.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the price and quantity after a per-unit tax, and say who bears it and what it destroys.

recap.keyIdea: A per-unit tax splits the price into what buyers pay and what sellers keep. It raises revenue on units still sold, destroys surplus on units that stop trading, and falls more on the side that finds it harder to walk away.

blocks.text: Back at the coffee market, the £6 tax left buyers paying £24 and sellers keeping £18. It raised £312 and destroyed £24 of surplus. In the gym market buyers carried only £2 of the £6, because they could walk away more easily than sellers.

recap.nextHook: A tax is one way to change a market. A price control is another, and it can leave a queue of buyers or a pile of stock nobody wants, so the next lesson looks at price controls and at costs that fall on people outside the trade.

lessons.title: Controls and spillovers

steps.headline: A ceiling below the market price

lead.text: Last lesson a tax changed a market from the outside. Another tool is to fix the price itself. A price ceiling is a legal maximum price, and a price floor is a legal minimum. Whether either one matters depends on where it sits compared with the price the market would reach by itself.

Go back to the lolly stall, where demand is Qd = 60 − 5P and supply is Qs = 5P, so the market settles at £6 and 30 lollies. The council sets a ceiling of £4. At that price buyers want 60 − 20 = 40 lollies, but sellers offer only 5 × 4 = 20. The ceiling is below the market price, so it binds: it holds the price down, and buyers want more than sellers will supply. The gap of 20 lollies is a shortage.

afterFigure.text: A sale needs a willing buyer and a willing seller, so only 20 lollies change hands, fewer than the 30 sold freely. The 20 buyers who miss out are left in a queue. Price no longer decides who gets a lolly, so something else has to, usually the order people arrive in or who they know.
A ceiling above £6, such as the £9 in the second case, would change nothing, because the market price is already below it. Only a control that stops the market reaching its own price has any effect.

lead.text: The council's £10 limit on tickets is a ceiling. Think about who decides how many tickets change hands at a capped price.
In the coffee market a ceiling of £12 sits below the equilibrium price. Compare what buyers want with what sellers offer at £12.

reveal.text: You compared the two quantities at the controlled price. Only 28 cups change hands, fewer than the 60 at equilibrium, so queues and connections ration the cups instead of price.

steps.headline: A floor above the market price

lead.text: A price floor works from the other side. A floor above the market price binds, because it holds the price up. At the lolly stall a floor of £8 means buyers want 60 − 40 = 20 lollies, while sellers, tempted by the high price, offer 5 × 8 = 40. The 20 lollies in between are a surplus: goods on offer that nobody buys.

afterFigure.text: As with the ceiling, the smaller quantity decides how much is sold. Here buyers are the short side, so only 20 lollies change hands, again fewer than at the free price. Sellers who made the other 20 are left with stock.

A floor below £6, like the £4 in the second case, would change nothing, just as a ceiling above £6 did not. A control that binds always shrinks trade below what the free market would have done, and it leaves one side of the market wanting more than it can get.

steps.headline: Coffee has Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20. A floor of £26 is set. How many cups go unsold?

workedSteps.text: Compare the floor with the equilibrium price of £20. It sits above, so it binds.
Find the cups buyers want at £26.
Find the cups sellers offer at £26.
Subtract.

steps.headline: The floor is raised to £30. How many cups go unsold?

workedSteps.text: £30 is above the equilibrium price, so the floor binds.
Find the cups sellers offer at £30.
Find the cups buyers want at £30.
Subtract demand from supply.

steps.headline: A cost nobody is billed for

lead.text: Prices can also go wrong in a quieter way. Take a fertiliser plant whose run-off pollutes a stream below it. Each tonne costs the plant money for materials and labour. Each tonne also does £2 of damage to the fishermen downstream, and the plant never sees that £2, because nobody sends it a bill. A cost borne by people outside the sale is called an external cost.

A market settles on the costs the firm actually pays and the values buyers actually place on the good. In the market with demand Qd = 60 − 5P and supply Qs = 5P, that means £6 and 30 tonnes. The 30th tonne is worth £6 to its buyer and costs the plant £6 to make, so the market sees no reason to stop there. But it also does £2 of damage, so it costs society £8.

afterFigure.text: So some of the 30 tonnes are worth less to buyers than they cost everyone together. The market counts only the cost the firm pays, so it makes more than is worth making. The next question checks that reading, and the screen after it counts the damage properly.

lead.text: Use the idea from the last screen on a paint firm: the damage to neighbours is in nobody's accounts.

steps.headline: Counting the damage

lead.text: To count the damage, add it to each tonne's cost. The firm's supply curve shows what each tonne costs the firm. What each tonne costs society is higher by the damage per tonne, so the social supply equation has P minus the damage wherever the firm's has P.
In the fertiliser market a £2 damage turns Qs = 5P into 5(P − 2) = 5P − 10. Setting that equal to demand gives 60 − 5P = 5P − 10, so 70 = 10P and P = 7. The quantity is 60 − 35 = 25 tonnes.

afterFigure.text: The efficient quantity is 25 tonnes, which is 5 fewer than the market makes. Each of those 5 tonnes is worth less to its buyer than it costs once the damage is added. The figure puts the plant's own cost curve beside the social one, and a larger damage lifts it further above and cuts the efficient quantity more. The algebra is the same as for a £2 tax in the last lesson, and that is no accident.

lead.text: Paint firms' own costs give Qs = 4P − 20, and each tonne does £9 of damage. Add the damage to supply, then meet demand.

reveal.text: Counting the damage lifts the cost curve by £9. Social supply meets demand at £26 and 48 tonnes, 12 fewer than the market makes.

steps.headline: What the overproduction costs

lead.text: Go back to the fertiliser plant, which makes 30 tonnes when 25 would be efficient. On each of the 5 extra tonnes, the cost to society exceeds the value to the buyer. For the 26th tonne the excess is small, and by the 30th tonne it has grown to the full £2 of damage. These losses form a triangle with base 5 and height 2, so the loss is ½ × 5 × 2 = £5. It is the deadweight loss of the unregulated market.

A tax that puts the damage on the firm's own bill removes it. Charge the plant £2 for each tonne, equal to the damage, and its costs now match society's, so it makes 25 tonnes. This is called a Pigouvian tax, after Arthur Pigou, the economist who proposed it in his 1920 book The Economics of Welfare.

afterFigure.text: Unlike the tax in the last lesson, this one does not lose surplus. The trades it stops are the ones that were not worth making once the damage was counted, so removing them leaves society better off.

lead.text: In the paint market the damage is £9 a tonne. Measure what making too much costs.

reveal.text: On the 12 extra tonnes the gap between social cost and buyers' value grows from nothing at 48 to £9 at 60: a triangle of £54.

lessons.orientation: Predict shortages and surpluses from price controls, and correct an external cost with a Pigouvian tax.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A city is hosting a sold-out concert, and tickets are changing hands at high prices. The council answers with a law: no ticket may be sold for more than £10. Fans cheer, since the price they were paying was much higher.

A price is a message as well as a bill. It tells buyers how much to take and sellers how much to offer, and a law that overrides it can leave the two sides wanting different amounts. Prices can also be wrong in a quieter way, when a firm's choices harm people outside the sale and nobody sends the firm the bill.

This lesson looks at both. We work out what a legal maximum and a legal minimum do to a market, then turn to a cost that falls on neighbours and see how a tax can put it back on the firm that causes it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict shortages and surpluses from price controls, and correct a cost that falls on other people.

recap.keyIdea: A control that binds stops buyers and sellers trading as they want: a ceiling creates a shortage, a floor a surplus. A cost that falls on others makes a market overproduce, and a tax equal to the damage corrects it.

blocks.text: Back at the concert, the £10 ceiling meant 300 tickets sold while more fans wanted one. In the coffee market you found a shortage of 48 cups under a £12 ceiling and 60 unsold under a £30 floor. The paint market overproduced by 12 tonnes, a loss of £54.

recap.nextHook: Throughout these lessons the costs of supply came as a given equation. The next lesson opens up a firm to see where its costs come from and how they decide how much it makes.

lessons.title: Costs and the best output

steps.headline: Costs that move and costs that don't

lead.text: Costs fall into two kinds. A fixed cost is one the firm pays whatever it makes, such as rent. A variable cost grows with output, such as paper, flour or wages paid by the hour. Adding the two gives total cost, the full bill for a given amount of output.

Take a print shop that pays £50 rent a day and spends £1 on paper and ink for every poster. If it prints nothing, its total cost is still the £50 of rent. If it prints 20 posters, the variable cost is 20 × £1 = £20 and the total cost is £50 + £20 = £70.

The difference matters when a firm makes decisions. The rent has to be paid whatever the firm chooses, but each extra poster brings a cost with it. A sensible choice about how much to print looks at the costs the choice itself changes, and the next two screens turn that idea into two measures.

steps.headline: The cost of each unit

lead.text: The first measure is the cost of a typical unit. Average total cost is total cost divided by the number of units made. Take a workshop that pays £36 rent a day. Other costs climb as the room fills, so making q units adds q² on top of the rent. Total cost is then TC = 36 + q².

Two units cost 36 + 4 = £40 in total, an average of £20 each. Six units cost 36 + 36 = £72, an average of £12. Twelve units cost 36 + 144 = £180, an average of £15. The cost per unit falls and then rises.

afterFigure.text: The fall comes from the rent. With only 2 units each one carries £18 of it, and with 6 units each carries £6. The rise comes from crowding, which makes every unit beyond the sixth cost more to squeeze in. The two effects balance at 6 units, where the average is lowest.
The figure shows this workshop and one with £100 rent. The higher rent pushes the lowest point to a larger output.

lead.text: Take the bakery from the start of the lesson. Each loaf also uses £2 of flour, and the rent is shared across the loaves baked that day.

steps.headline: The cost of one more

lead.text: Average cost smooths everything into one number per unit. A firm deciding whether to make one more unit needs something sharper. Marginal cost is the extra cost of making that one more unit, which is the change in total cost when output goes up by one.

In the workshop, going from 5 to 6 units lifts total cost from 36 + 25 = £61 to £72, so the sixth unit has a marginal cost of £11. The seventh takes it from £72 to £85, which is £13. Marginal cost rises with output here, and the line MC = 2q runs through the middle of those two figures, at £12 for 6 units. This course uses MC = 2q for the workshop.

afterFigure.text: Marginal cost and average cost are linked. If the next unit costs less than the average so far, adding it pulls the average down. If it costs more, it pulls the average up. At 2 units the marginal cost is about £4 against an average of £20, so the average is being pulled down. At 12 units it is about £24 against £15, so the average is being pulled up.
The average stops falling at the output where marginal cost has risen to meet it. For the workshop that is 6 units, where marginal cost is £12 and so is the average.

lead.text: Marginal cost is read from a table of total costs by subtracting each total from the one after it.

steps.headline: A workshop pays £400 rent, with variable cost q². At what output is average total cost lowest?

workedSteps.text: Write marginal cost and average total cost.
Average cost is lowest where marginal cost meets it.
Take q from both sides.
Solve.

steps.headline: With £100 rent and variable cost q², find the output where average total cost is lowest.

workedSteps.text: Write marginal cost and average total cost.
Set them equal and simplify.
Solve for the output.
Put that output into ATC.

steps.headline: How much to make at a given price

lead.text: Now the choice itself. A firm in a very large market cannot move the price by changing its own output, so it takes the price as given. Such a firm is called a price-taker. Every extra unit it sells brings in exactly the market price, and the revenue that one more unit adds is called marginal revenue. For a price-taker, marginal revenue equals the price.

The rule follows from comparing marginal revenue with marginal cost. While a unit adds more revenue than cost, making it raises profit. Once it adds more cost than revenue, making it lowers profit. Marginal cost rises with output, so there is a single best output, where marginal cost has just risen to the price.

afterFigure.text: Try it on the £36 workshop at a price of £20. Setting 20 = 2q gives q = 10. Revenue is 20 × 10 = £200 and total cost is 36 + 100 = £136, so profit is £64.
