A unit beyond 10 would add about £22 of cost for £20 of revenue, and a unit short of 10 would leave money on the table. The figure marks the best output at two prices.

lead.text: The same test works on a single unit. Compare what the unit adds to revenue with what it adds to cost.
The workshop with £100 rent has marginal cost MC = 2q and now sells at £30 a unit. Choose the output that makes the most profit.

reveal.text: Below 15 units the next unit adds more revenue than cost; beyond 15 it adds less. That is the marginal rule from the start of the course, applied to output.

steps.headline: When the price will not cover the rent

lead.text: A falling price tests the rule. At a lower price the best output is smaller, and revenue may no longer cover total cost, which leaves the firm with a loss. The natural question is whether it should close.

In the short run the rent has to be paid whether or not the firm makes anything, so closing does not avoid it. Take the £36 workshop at a price of £8. Setting 8 = 2q gives q = 4. Revenue is 8 × 4 = £32 and total cost is 36 + 16 = £52, a loss of £20. Closing would lose the whole £36 of rent.

afterFigure.text: The comparison shows why it carries on. The £32 of revenue covers the £16 of variable cost and puts £16 towards the rent, which cuts the loss from £36 to £20. A firm should keep producing while revenue covers its variable costs, and should close only if the price falls so low that it does not. The next question puts the other workshop in the same position.

lead.text: The market price falls to £16. Find the best output again, and then see whether it still pays.

reveal.text: A loss of £36 is still better than shutting down, which would lose the whole £100 of rent. In the short run the firm keeps producing.

lessons.orientation: Separate fixed, variable, average and marginal cost, and choose output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A bakery pays £60 rent every day, whether it bakes ten loaves or a hundred. Flour is different, because every extra loaf needs more of it. So a day's baking costs two kinds of money, one that never moves and one that grows with every loaf.

That mix gives the cost of each loaf an odd shape. Bake only a few and every loaf carries a large share of the rent. Bake many and the rent is spread thin, until the kitchen is so crowded that squeezing in one more loaf starts to cost a lot.

So far in this course each market came with a supply equation already written. This lesson opens up the firm behind it. It separates the kinds of cost, finds the output at which a unit is cheapest to make, and then uses the cost of one extra unit to decide how much to make when the market price is fixed.

intro.promise: By the end you'll separate fixed, average and marginal cost, and pick the output that makes a price-taking firm the most profit.

recap.keyIdea: Average total cost is the cost per unit; marginal cost is the cost of one more. A price-taking firm makes the most profit where price equals marginal cost.

blocks.text: The bakery's average cost came to £4 a loaf at 30 loaves. For the workshop with £100 rent, the cost per unit bottomed out at 10 units and profit peaked at 15 units, earning £125. At a price of £16 the firm lost £36 but still beat shutting down.

recap.nextHook: Every firm in this lesson took its price from the market. The next lesson looks at a firm with no rivals, which has to choose its price and so changes the answer.

lessons.title: One seller

steps.headline: One boat, one price

lead.text: A firm that is the only seller of what it sells is called a monopolist. The ferry owner is one: nobody else sells the crossing, so she does not take a price from a market. She sets it, and a firm that sets its own price is a price-maker. That does not leave her free to charge anything. At £60 hardly anyone would cross and at £5 almost everyone would, so the number of tickets she sells depends on the price she names.

That link is the demand curve from the earlier lessons, now seen from the seller's side. Say the island's demand is P = 50 − Q, where Q is the number of tickets sold in a day. Priced at £40, the boat carries 10 passengers; priced at £39, it carries 11. Carrying a passenger costs her £14 in fuel and wear on the boat, the same for everyone.
To pick a price she needs to know what an extra passenger is worth to her. The obvious answer is the ticket price, and it turns out to be wrong. The next screen shows why.

steps.headline: What one more passenger adds

lead.text: Suppose she charges £40, so 10 passengers cross and she takes in 10 × £40 = £400. To fill an eleventh seat she must drop the price to £39. The boat has one price for everyone, so all 11 pay £39 and her takings become 11 × £39 = £429. The extra passenger raised her takings by £29, which is well below the £39 ticket.

The shortfall has a simple cause. The new passenger pays £39, but the ten who were already travelling now pay £1 less each, and that costs her £10. So the extra revenue is £39 − £10 = £29. The extra revenue from selling one more unit is called marginal revenue. For the price-taking firms of the last lesson it equalled the price, because selling more never moved the price. A monopolist's price falls whenever she sells more, so her marginal revenue is always below the price.
The more passengers already travelling, the more each price cut costs, and the further marginal revenue drops below the price.
Use the same split as on the ferry: what the new unit sells for, less what the price cut costs on the units already selling.

steps.headline: A line for marginal revenue

lead.text: Working this out one price at a time is slow, and for a straight demand curve there is a shortcut. With demand P = 50 − Q, the next ticket after Q sales pays about 50 − Q. Each extra ticket lowers the price by £1, and that £1 comes off all Q tickets already sold, which costs about £Q. That leaves 50 − Q − Q = 50 − 2Q.

In general, for demand P = a − bQ, marginal revenue is MR = a − 2bQ. It starts at the same price as demand and falls twice as fast. The figure draws both lines for the ferry, with a flat line for the £14 cost of carrying a passenger.

afterFigure.text: At 10 passengers the line gives £30, and the step from 10 to 11 was £29, which sits between the line's £30 at 10 and £28 at 11. The line reaches zero at 25 passengers, while demand does not reach zero until 50. The gold dot marks where the owner should stop selling, and the next screens show how to find it.

lead.text: A different seller faces demand P = 100 − Q. Use the marginal revenue line to find what its next unit is worth, and compare that with the price.

reveal.text: Marginal revenue is £40 while the price is £70. Each extra unit is worth much less to the seller than the price on the tag.

steps.headline: Where the owner stops selling

lead.text: Marginal revenue gives the owner something to weigh against her £14 cost. The rule is the one from the last lesson: a passenger is worth carrying while the sale adds more to her takings than to her costs. The sale adds marginal revenue, not the ticket price, so that is what she compares with £14.

With MR = 50 − 2Q the comparison is quick. With 10 passengers MR is £30, so another sale pays. Once there are 15 it is £20, which still pays. Reaching 18 it equals the £14 cost, and by 20 it has fallen to £10, so a sale there loses money. She stops where marginal revenue meets marginal cost: 50 − 2Q = 14, which gives Q = 18.

The price comes from demand. The 18 passengers will each pay 50 − 18 = £32, so that is the ticket price. She takes in 18 × £32 = £576, spends 18 × £14 = £252 and keeps £324. Comparing the price with the cost would have misled her. At 20 passengers the price is £30, far above £14, yet the twentieth sale adds only about £10.

steps.headline: Demand is P = 120 − 2Q and marginal cost is £40. What output and price maximise the monopolist's profit?

workedSteps.text: Marginal revenue falls twice as fast as demand.
Set marginal revenue equal to marginal cost.
Solve for the output.
Read the price from the demand curve.

steps.headline: Demand is P = 100 − Q and marginal cost is £20. What output and price maximise profit?

workedSteps.text: Marginal revenue falls twice as fast as demand.
Set it equal to marginal cost and solve.
Read the price from the demand curve.

lead.text: A new demand curve and cost. Write the marginal revenue line first, then set it equal to marginal cost.

reveal.text: You doubled the demand slope to get marginal revenue, then solved. At 12 units the monopolist charges £36.

steps.headline: What the island loses

lead.text: Now suppose the crossing were shared among many small boats, all competing for passengers. As the last lesson showed, sellers in competition end up charging the cost of one more unit, here £14. Demand P = 50 − Q gives 50 − Q = 14, so 36 passengers cross. The monopolist carries only 18 and charges £32.
So she sells half as many tickets at more than twice the competitive price. The figure shades the passengers in between.

afterFigure.text: Between 18 and 36 passengers, every crossing is worth more to the passenger than the £14 it costs to carry them. The nineteenth would pay up to £31 for a trip that costs £14. These trades never happen, because carrying the extra passenger means cutting the price for everyone and that costs her more than the passenger adds.

The lost value forms a triangle with base 36 − 18 = 18 and height £32 − £14 = £18, so its area is ½ × 18 × 18 = £162. It is the deadweight loss of monopoly, the same idea as the loss from a tax. Her £324 profit is value moved from passengers to her, but the £162 goes to nobody.

lead.text: The monopolist in the faded example faced P = 100 − Q with a marginal cost of £20 and sold 40 units. Find what competition would sell in the same market.
Now compare that monopoly with competition. Count the units that competition would sell and the monopoly does not.

reveal.text: The lost value is a triangle with base 40 and height £40: £800. The monopoly's profit is a transfer from buyers to the firm; the £800 is lost to everyone.

lessons.orientation: Derive a single seller's marginal revenue and use it to find its price and output. Then measure the deadweight loss of monopoly.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Every firm in the last lesson took its price from the market. A workshop could make as many units as it liked and each one sold at the going price, because it was one maker among many. Its only decision was how much to make.

Now take an island with a single ferry to the mainland, run by one family. Nobody else sells the crossing, so nobody can undercut her. The owner names a price and the islanders decide how many tickets to buy at it. A higher price keeps some people at home. A lower price fills the boat but brings in less from each passenger.

She has two things to settle, how much to charge and how many crossings to sell, and the two are linked. This lesson follows her decision. It starts with what an extra passenger really adds to her takings. From there it finds where she stops selling, and then it measures what that choice costs the island compared with ferries in competition.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find a single seller's price and output from marginal revenue, and measure the value its pricing wastes.

recap.keyIdea: A monopolist's marginal revenue falls below its price, so it stops where MR meets MC and charges what demand allows. That is less output at a higher price than competition, and the units in between are a deadweight loss.

blocks.text: You found marginal revenue of £40 against a £70 price, and the ferry owner stopped at 18 passengers where competition would carry 36. In the £100 market the monopoly sold 40 units where competition sold 80, and £800 of value was lost.

recap.nextHook: The ferry owner had no rivals to watch. Next we look at a few firms that share a market, where each one's best choice depends on what the others do.

lessons.title: Strategic choices

steps.headline: Two cafés, one decision

lead.text: Before the phone networks, a smaller case where the numbers are easy to follow. Two cafés, Ruby's and Sol's, face each other across one street. Each owner decides every evening whether to close early or stay open late. Each choice is called a strategy, and what a café earns depends on both owners' strategies together.

A table keeps track of this. The rows are Ruby's strategies and the columns are Sol's. Each cell holds a pair of numbers, Ruby's profit first and Sol's second, in thousands of pounds a week. Such a table is called a payoff matrix, and a payoff is what a player earns from an outcome.

afterFigure.text: Read the top-left cell first. If both cafés close early, each makes £8k. In the bottom-left cell Ruby stays open late while Sol closes early, so Ruby takes the late trade: £12k for her and only £3k for him. In the bottom-right cell both stay open late. They split the late trade and each pays for staff and lighting, so each makes £6k. The second case is a quieter street, with the same shape and smaller numbers.

steps.headline: The best reply to a choice

lead.text: Now sit in Ruby's seat. She does not know what Sol will do, but she can ask a smaller question: for each thing Sol might do, which of her two strategies pays more? Answering for one choice at a time is easy, because only one column of the table matters.

Suppose Sol closes early. In that column Ruby earns £8k by closing early too and £12k by staying open, so staying open is better. Suppose instead Sol stays open late. Now Ruby earns £3k by closing early and £6k by staying open, so staying open is better again. The strategy that pays a player most against a given choice by the rival is called her best response to it.
Finding a best response always works the same way. Hold the rival's choice fixed, then compare your own payoffs. The next question gives you that job in a different table.
Two phone networks, Alpha and Beta, each set a High or a Low monthly price. Hold one of Beta's choices fixed and compare Alpha's payoffs against it.

steps.headline: A strategy that wins either way

lead.text: Ruby's answer was the same both times. Staying open late was her best response when Sol closed early and her best response when Sol stayed open. A strategy that is the best response to every choice the rival might make is called a dominant strategy. Its advantage is that a player does not have to guess what the rival will do, because the same strategy is best either way.
Sol's payoffs mirror Ruby's, so staying open late is dominant for him too. The figure marks the best responses in each column and row.

afterFigure.text: Not every game gives a player a dominant strategy. If one strategy wins against one choice and loses against another, the player has to guess. Here both owners have one, so neither needs to guess and both stay open late, earning £6k each. That is less than the £8k each would earn if both closed early, and a later screen returns to that.

lead.text: Back to the phone networks. Alpha's payoffs are in the matrix. Find which price pays Alpha more against each of Beta's choices, and decide whether one price wins both times.

reveal.text: You tested Alpha's best response against both of Beta's choices. When one strategy wins both times it is dominant, and Alpha needs no forecast of Beta.

steps.headline: A stable outcome

lead.text: Both cafés have a dominant strategy, so we can say where they end up: both open late. Look at that bottom-right cell from the inside. If Ruby alone closed early she would drop from £6k to £3k, and if Sol alone closed early he would drop the same way. Neither gains by changing their own choice while the other holds still, so neither moves.

An outcome with that property is called a Nash equilibrium, after the mathematician John Nash. In it each player's strategy is a best response to the other's. The test is the one you have been using: take a cell and let each player switch alone in turn. If neither gains, the cell is an equilibrium.

afterFigure.text: Some games have more than one equilibrium. Take two drivers who meet on a narrow road, each choosing to keep left or keep right. If both keep left, or both keep right, they pass safely. If they choose different sides they collide. Both-left and both-right are each stable, because a driver who switches alone causes a crash. A mismatch is not stable, because a driver in it gains by switching to the other's side.

steps.headline: Price war: Alpha and Beta each choose High or Low. Find the Nash equilibrium.

workedSteps.text: Find Alpha's best response to each of Beta's choices.
workedSteps.math: Against High: Low pays 14, High pays 10. Against Low: Low pays 5, High pays 2.

workedSteps.text: Beta's payoffs mirror Alpha's, so Low is Beta's best response as well.
Both play Low, and each earns 5.

steps.headline: Two makers each choose plug standard A or B. Matching on A pays 6 each; matching on B pays 4 each; a mismatch pays nothing. Find the Nash equilibria.

workedSteps.text: At A/A, suppose Maker A switches alone to B while Maker B stays on A.
That is below the 6 A earned, so A/A is an equilibrium. B/B works the same way: a lone switch drops a maker from 4 to nothing.
A mismatched cell is not an equilibrium: a maker there earns nothing and gains by switching.
Count the cells where neither maker gains by switching alone.

steps.headline: A trap with a name

lead.text: Look again at the cafés' equilibrium. Both stay open late and each earns £6k. If both had closed early, each would have earned £8k, so both would be better off. Yet neither will close early, because whichever way the other goes, closing early alone pays less. The equilibrium is stable, and it is worse for both players than another outcome they could have reached.

A game with this shape is called a prisoner's dilemma. The name comes from the story of two suspects held in separate rooms. Each is better off confessing whatever the other does, yet if both confess they do worse than if both stayed silent.

Rival firms can fall into the same trap. They could agree to keep prices high, but each would be tempted to undercut, and a firm that keeps to the agreement while the other undercuts loses most. The next question looks at the price war between the phone networks, where that happens.
Back in the price war, both firms play their dominant strategy. Look up what each earns there and add the two together.

reveal.text: Both choose Low and earn £5m each, £10m together, though High/High would give £20m. Each firm's best choice leaves both worse off: a prisoner's dilemma.

steps.headline: Meeting again and again

lead.text: So far the cafés and the networks met once. Most rivals meet again, and that changes what a choice means. Staying open late undercuts Sol today, but he can remember it. A game played over several rounds by the same players is called a repeated game.

In a repeated game a player can react to what the rival did before. One simple rule is tit for tat: be friendly in the first round, then copy whatever the rival did in the round before. Against a friendly rival it stays friendly. Against one who undercuts, it undercuts back from the next round on.

afterFigure.text: Take three rounds. If Ruby plays tit for tat and Sol always stays open late, round one costs Ruby: she closes early for £3k while Sol takes £12k. After that she copies him, so rounds two and three are open against open at £6k each. Her total is 3 + 6 + 6 = £15k, against £18k if she had stayed open all three rounds. If both play tit for tat, both close early every round and each earns 3 × £8k = £24k. The threat of being copied is what makes the friendly choice pay, so repetition can make cooperation worthwhile.

cases.label: Ruby tit for tat v Sol always open late

lead.text: Now the phone networks meet for five rounds. Alpha plays tit for tat: High first, then it copies Beta's last move. Beta always sets Low.

reveal.text: Alpha is undercut once, then matches Low: £22m, while Beta earns £34m. Against another tit-for-tat player Alpha would earn £10m a round. When a game repeats, the threat of retaliation can make cooperation pay.

cases.label: Tit for tat v always Low
Tit for tat v tit for tat

lessons.orientation: Find best responses, dominant strategies and Nash equilibria in payoff matrices, and see how repetition supports cooperation.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The ferry owner in the last lesson had to think about her buyers and nobody else. Her price was hers to choose and no rival could answer it. Most firms are not so lucky. A phone network or an airline on a busy route shares its market with a few rivals, and what any one of them earns depends on what the others do.

Take two networks, Alpha and Beta, that serve one town. Each is about to set a monthly price, High or Low. If both charge High, both do well. If Alpha charges Low while Beta stays High, Alpha takes customers from Beta and does better still, while Beta's profit falls. Beta has the same thought about Alpha, and each knows the other is thinking it.

So neither can settle on a price alone. This lesson gives a way to reason about that. It starts with a table of every combination of choices, uses the table to find what each firm should do, and ends with what changes when the same firms meet again.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict what two rival firms will choose, and say why meeting repeatedly can make cooperation pay.

recap.keyIdea: Your best choice depends on the other player's. A Nash equilibrium is where nobody gains by switching alone, and it can leave everyone worse off, as in a prisoner's dilemma. Repetition can make cooperation pay, because a rival can punish.

blocks.text: You found Low dominant for both networks, so they earned £10m between them instead of £20m. A tit-for-tat Alpha still took £22m over five rounds against a rival who always cut.

recap.nextHook: That is the last lesson of the course. The tools work best together, so pick a market you know and ask who sets its price, and what each seller would do if a rival moved first.

questions.prompt: Workshop A can make at most 60 chairs or 20 tables a week, trading one for the other at a constant rate. How many chairs does each extra table cost?
hints: Both maximums use the same week of work.
Ask how many chairs one table's share of the week could have made.
Divide the maximum number of chairs by the maximum number of tables.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 60 chairs ÷ 20 tables = 3 chairs per table.

questions.onCorrect: 3 chairs. A table's opportunity cost is the chairs the same slice of the week could have made: 60 ÷ 20.

misconceptions.feedback: 20 is the most tables the week allows. The question asks how many chairs one table replaces.
That is every chair the week could make. One table uses only its slice of the week.
The goods trade at a ratio, so subtracting the maximums does not work. Compare them by dividing.

questions.prompt: Workshop A can make at most 60 chairs or 20 tables a week at a constant rate. It makes 30 chairs and 5 tables. Where does that point lie?
hints: Work out how many tables the time left after 30 chairs could make.

acceptedIdeas: Inside the frontier
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Thirty chairs leave time for 10 tables, so 5 tables wastes capacity: the point is inside the frontier.

choices.label: Inside the frontier
On the frontier
Beyond the frontier

questions.onCorrect: Inside. 30 chairs use half the week, which could make 10 tables, so making 5 leaves time idle.

misconceptions.feedback: On the frontier means all the week is used. Work out how many tables the time left after 30 chairs could make.
Beyond the frontier needs more time than the week holds. Check how much of the week 30 chairs use.

questions.prompt: Machines given up in moving from 40 to 60 food
hints: Only the machines column matters for what is given up.
Find machines at both points.
Subtract the later figure from the earlier one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Machines fall from 70 to 40: 70 − 40 = 30 machines for 20 more food.

questions.onCorrect: Machines fall from 70 to 40, so 30 machines are given up for 20 more food.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the machines at the starting point. What is given up is the fall between the two points.
That is the machines at the end point. Take the change from start to end.
That is the food gained. The question asks about machines.

questions.prompt: On a country's bowed frontier, food rises from 60 to 80 units while machines fall from 40 to 0. What is the opportunity cost per unit of food, measured in machines?
hints: Find the machines lost on this step.
Find the food gained on this step.
Divide the loss by the gain.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 40 machines ÷ 20 food = 2 machines per unit of food.

questions.onCorrect: 2 machines per unit. The step from 60 to 80 food costs more per unit than the step before it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the machines lost in total. Divide by the food gained to price one unit.
That is the food gained, not the machines given up per unit.
That averages over the whole frontier. Use only the step from 60 to 80 food.

questions.prompt: Priya has 12 hours of study time. An essay takes her 3 hours and a problem set takes 1.5 hours. What is the opportunity cost of one essay, measured in problem sets?
hints: An essay uses up a fixed block of time.
Ask how many problem sets fit into that same block.
Divide the essay's time by the time for one problem set.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 3 ÷ 1.5 = 2 problem sets per essay. The 12-hour total does not change the rate.

questions.onCorrect: 2 problem sets. An essay's cost is the other task's output over the same time; the 12-hour total does not change the rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how many essays 12 hours allow. Compare one essay's time with one problem set's time.
That is a problem set's cost in essays, the wrong way up.
That is every problem set 12 hours could hold. One essay uses only its own block of time.

questions.prompt: A production possibilities frontier bows outward from the origin. What does that shape show about the opportunity cost of the good on the horizontal axis?
hints: Compare how steep the frontier is near each axis.

acceptedIdeas: Increasing opportunity cost
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each extra unit of one good costs more of the other, as resources less suited to it are moved across.

choices.label: Increasing opportunity cost
Constant opportunity cost
Falling opportunity cost

questions.onCorrect: Each extra unit of one good costs more of the other, because resources less suited to it are moved across.

misconceptions.feedback: A constant cost gives a straight line, not a bow.
Falling cost would bend the frontier inward, towards the origin.

questions.prompt: In a day Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes. What is her opportunity cost of one cake, in loaves?
hints: A day of cakes and a day of bread use the same time.
Ask how much bread one cake's share of the day could have made.
Divide her loaves per day by her cakes per day.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 12 loaves ÷ 6 cakes = 2 loaves per cake.

questions.onCorrect: 2 loaves. A cake's opportunity cost is the loaves the same time could have made: 12 ÷ 6.

misconceptions.feedback: That is every loaf her day could make. One cake uses only its share of the day.
That is the most cakes she can bake. The question asks how many loaves one cake replaces.
That is a loaf's cost in cakes, the wrong way up.

questions.prompt: In a day Ana can bake 12 loaves or 6 cakes; Ben can bake 6 loaves or 4 cakes. Who gives up fewer loaves to bake a cake? Give the name.
hints: Price a cake in loaves for each baker.
Ana makes more cakes, but ask what each one gives up.

acceptedIdeas: Ben
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Ben. A cake costs him 1.5 loaves against Ana's 2.

questions.onCorrect: Ben. A cake costs him 6 ÷ 4 loaves, less than Ana's 12 ÷ 6.

misconceptions.feedback: Ana bakes more cakes, but the question is about what she gives up. Price a cake in loaves for each baker.

questions.prompt: How many more loaves does he end with than before?
hints: Find how many loaves the swap brings him.
He keeps the same number of cakes as before.
Subtract the loaves he used to bake from the loaves he receives.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: He receives 2 × 1.75 = 3.5 loaves and keeps 2 cakes, so he has 3.5 − 3 = 0.5 loaves more.

questions.onCorrect: 0.5 loaves more. He keeps the same 2 cakes and ends with 3.5 loaves instead of 3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is all the loaves he receives. Take off the 3 he used to bake.
That is the price of one cake. He swaps two, and he already had loaves before.

questions.prompt: Cara can bake 8 loaves or 4 cakes a day; Dan can bake 4 loaves or 2 cakes. By how many loaves does their opportunity cost of a cake differ?
hints: Work out each person's loaves per cake.
Compare the two rates.
Subtract the smaller from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each gives up 8 ÷ 4 = 4 ÷ 2 loaves per cake, so the costs are equal and the difference is nothing.

questions.onCorrect: None. Both give up 2 loaves per cake, so no price can leave both better off.

misconceptions.feedback: That is each person's cost, not the difference between the costs.
That is how many cakes Cara can bake. Compare the loaves each gives up per cake.

questions.prompt: In an hour Mira can code 4 web pages or write 8 reports. Tom can code 1 page or write 4 reports. What is Tom's opportunity cost of one page, in reports?
hints: Use only Tom's two figures.
Ask how many reports he forgoes to spend an hour on pages.
Divide his reports per hour by his pages per hour.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Tom gives up 4 reports ÷ 1 page = 4 reports per page; Mira gives up only 2.

questions.onCorrect: 4 reports. Tom's cost of a page is the reports his hour could have produced: 4 ÷ 1.

misconceptions.feedback: That is pages per report, the wrong way up.
That is Mira's cost of a page. The question asks about Tom.
The goods trade at a ratio, so subtracting does not work. Divide instead.

questions.prompt: Mira gives up 2 reports per web page; Tom gives up 4. Which division of work produces gains from trade?
hints: Give each task to the person who gives up less to do it.

acceptedIdeas: Mira codes pages and Tom writes reports
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mira has the lower opportunity cost of pages, so she codes them; Tom's lower cost of reports makes him the report writer.

choices.label: Mira codes pages and Tom writes reports
Tom codes pages and Mira writes reports
Each splits the hour equally

questions.onCorrect: Mira codes pages and Tom writes reports: each does the job they give up less for, and both gain from trade.

misconceptions.feedback: Tom gives up more reports for each page, so he is the dearer coder. Give each job to whoever gives up less.
Splitting the hour equally ignores who is cheaper at each job. Gains come from specialising.

questions.prompt: A café's extra opening hours have marginal benefits of £90, £70, £55, £40 and £30, and marginal costs of £30, £35, £45, £50 and £60. How many extra hours should it open?
hints: Compare benefit and cost hour by hour.
Keep adding hours while the next one brings at least as much as it costs.
Stop before the first hour whose cost exceeds its benefit.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Hours one to three each bring at least their cost (£90 > £30, £70 > £35, £55 > £45); the fourth brings £40 for £50.

questions.onCorrect: 3 hours. Each of the first three brings more than it costs; later hours would bring less than they cost.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the last hour you counted with its own cost. Does it still pay?
Hours are added only while they pay. Look for the first one that does not.
The first hour is the best deal, but later hours can still be worth opening.

questions.prompt: Total net benefit of the three hours, in pounds
hints: The net benefit of an hour is its benefit minus its cost.
Work out the net benefit of each of those hours.
Add them.
questions.onCorrect: £105. Add each hour's own net benefit.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the three benefits without taking the costs off.
That adds up the costs. Net benefit is benefit minus cost.

questions.prompt: The café's hours bring marginal benefits of £90, £70, £55, £40 and £30. Its marginal costs rise by £20 to £50, £55, £65, £70 and £80. How many extra hours should it now open?
hints: Use the new costs, hour by hour.
Compare each hour's benefit with its new cost, in order.
Count the hours whose benefit still covers the cost.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: £90 > £50 and £70 > £55, but £55 < £65, so it opens two hours.

questions.onCorrect: 2 hours. The third hour now brings less than it costs, so the stopping point moves earlier.

misconceptions.feedback: Use the new costs for every hour. Does the third still cover its own cost?
Hours are added only while they pay. Find the first one that does not.

questions.prompt: The fourth extra hour brings £40 of benefit and costs £50. By how many pounds does opening it change the café's net benefit?
hints: Subtract the hour's cost from its benefit.
Keep the sign, since a loss is negative.
Use that hour's figures only, not the averages.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: £40 − £50 = −£10: opening it makes the café worse off.

questions.onCorrect: −£10. Only the extra hour's own benefit and cost decide it, so opening the fourth makes the café worse off.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the average benefit of four hours. Only the fourth hour's own figures decide it.
Check the sign: this hour costs more than it brings.

questions.prompt: A student values successive hours of revision at 50, 40, 30, 20 and 10 points, and each hour costs her 25 points of other activities. How many hours should she revise?
hints: Every hour costs the same here.
Compare each hour's value with that cost in turn.
Count the hours worth more than the cost.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 50, 40 and 30 each exceed 25; the fourth hour's 20 does not.

questions.onCorrect: 3 hours. Revise while an hour is worth more than the other activities it displaces.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the last hour you counted with its cost. Is it still worth more?
Hours count only while they are worth more than they cost. Look for the first that is not.
Every hour costs the same, so later hours can still be worth it.

questions.prompt: A cost that has already been paid and cannot be recovered, whatever you decide next, is called what kind of cost? One word.
hints: Think of money that has gone for good, like a non-refundable ticket.

acceptedIdeas: sunk
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sunk. It is the same under every option, so it should not affect the choice.

questions.onCorrect: Sunk. It is the same under every option, so it should not affect the choice.

misconceptions.feedback: Marginal means the extra unit. The word you want describes money already gone for good.

questions.prompt: Demand for coffee is Qd = 100 − 2P, with P in pounds and Q in cups per day. How many cups are demanded at a price of £15?
hints: Substitute the price for P.
Multiply the price by the slope first.
Subtract that product from the intercept.
questions.onCorrect: 70 cups. Multiply the price by the slope, then take the result off the intercept.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 2 × 15. Take it off the intercept of 100.
That takes off the price only. Each £1 loses 2 cups.
That is the quantity at the higher price in the figure, not at £15.

questions.prompt: Equilibrium price, in pounds
hints: Set quantity demanded equal to quantity supplied.
Collect the P terms on one side and the numbers on the other.
Divide the gap between the intercepts by the sum of the slopes.
questions.onCorrect: £20. Set Qd equal to Qs, collect terms and divide by the combined slope.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the combined intercepts. Divide it by the combined slope.
That is the combined slope. Divide the intercepts by it.
That is the quantity traded, not the price.

questions.prompt: Cups traded per day
hints: Substitute the price into either equation.
Try the demand equation first.
Check that the supply equation gives the same number.
questions.onCorrect: 60 cups. Substitute the price into either equation; both give the same number.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price. Put it into an equation to find the quantity.
That is the demand intercept. Substitute the price to find the quantity.

questions.prompt: With Qd = 100 − 2P and Qs = 4P − 20, the price is stuck at £25. How many cups are offered but not bought each day?
hints: Find quantity demanded at that price.
Find quantity supplied at that price.
Subtract demand from supply.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Qs = 100 − 20 = 80 and Qd = 100 − 50 = 50, so 80 − 50 = 30 cups go unsold.

questions.onCorrect: 30 cups. At £25 sellers offer 80 and buyers want 50, so the excess goes unsold and pushes the price down.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what sellers offer. Subtract what buyers want.
That is what buyers want. Subtract it from what sellers offer.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 80 − 4P and supply is Qs = 8 + 2P. Find the equilibrium price in pounds.
hints: Set the two quantities equal.
Move the P terms together and the constants together.
Divide the constant difference by the combined slope.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 − 4P = 8 + 2P gives 72 = 6P, so P = £12 and Q = 32.

questions.onCorrect: £12. Set the quantities equal, then divide the constant gap by the combined slope.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between the constants. Divide it by the combined slope.
That is the quantity traded, not the price.
That is the combined slope. Divide the constants by it.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 150 − 5P and supply is Qs = 30 + 10P. Find the equilibrium quantity.
hints: Find the equilibrium price first.
Set the equations equal and solve for P.
Substitute that price back into either equation.
questions.onCorrect: 110 units. Solve for the price, then substitute it back into either equation.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the equilibrium price. Substitute it to find the quantity.
That is the gap between the constants. Solve for the price first, then find the quantity.

questions.prompt: The price of coffee rises while nothing else changes. What happens on the demand diagram for coffee?
hints: Ask which variable is measured on the axis of the curve itself.

acceptedIdeas: A movement along the demand curve
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The good's own price is on the axis, so a change in it moves buyers along the curve; quantity demanded falls.

choices.label: A movement along the demand curve
A leftward shift of the demand curve
A rightward shift of the demand curve

questions.onCorrect: A movement along the curve. The good's own price is on the axis, so changing it moves buyers along the curve.

misconceptions.feedback: A shift needs something other than the good's own price to change.
A shift needs something other than the good's own price to change.

questions.prompt: New equilibrium price, in pounds
hints: Set the new demand equal to the unchanged supply.
Collect the P terms on one side.
Divide the constant gap by the sum of the slopes.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 130 − 2P = 4P − 20 gives 150 = 6P, so P = £25, up from £20.

questions.onCorrect: £25. Set the new demand equal to the unchanged supply and solve.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the old price. Demand has shifted, so solve again with the new equation.
That is the constant gap. Divide it by the combined slope.
That is the quantity, not the price.

questions.prompt: A frost destroys coffee crops and sellers offer 24 fewer cups at every price: Qs = 4P − 44. Demand stays Qd = 100 − 2P. What is the new equilibrium quantity, in cups?
hints: Set the original demand equal to the new supply.
Solve for the price first.
Substitute that price into the demand equation.
questions.onCorrect: 52 cups. Supply shifted left: the price rises and the quantity falls.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the new price. The question asks for the quantity.
That is the old quantity. Supply has shifted, so solve again.

questions.prompt: Demand and supply each rise by 30 cups at every price: Qd = 130 − 2P and Qs = 4P + 10. By how many pounds does the equilibrium price change from its original £20?
hints: Find the new equilibrium price.
Set the new demand equal to the new supply and solve.
Subtract the old price from the new one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 130 − 2P = 4P + 10 gives P = £20, so the price is unchanged while quantity rises to 90.

questions.onCorrect: None. Both curves moved by the same amount, so quantity rose and the price stayed put.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how far each curve moved, not the change in price.
That is the new quantity, not the change in price.

questions.prompt: Tea and coffee are substitutes. The price of tea rises. What happens to the demand curve for coffee?
hints: Where might tea drinkers go when tea gets dearer?

acceptedIdeas: It shifts right.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Right: some tea drinkers switch to coffee, so more coffee is wanted at every coffee price.

choices.label: It shifts right.
It shifts left.
It does not move: this is a movement along it.

questions.onCorrect: Right. Some tea drinkers switch, so more coffee is wanted at every coffee price.

misconceptions.feedback: Some tea drinkers switch to coffee, so more is wanted at each coffee price, not less.
Tea's price is not on coffee's axis, so it moves the whole curve rather than a point along it.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 120 − 3P and supply is Qs = 2P. A new factory adds 20 units of supply at every price. What is the new equilibrium price, in pounds?
hints: Write the new supply equation.
Set it equal to demand.
Solve for P.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Supply becomes Qs = 20 + 2P; 120 − 3P = 20 + 2P gives 100 = 5P, so P = £20, down from £24.

questions.onCorrect: £20. New supply of 20 + 2P meets the unchanged demand at a lower price.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price before the new factory. Solve again with the new supply.
That is the constant gap. Divide it by the combined slope.

questions.prompt: When the price of a concert ticket falls from £11 to £9, the number sold rises from 35 to 65. Using the midpoint method, what is the absolute value of the price elasticity of demand?
hints: Divide the change in quantity by the average of the two quantities.
Divide the change in price by the average of the two prices.
Divide the first percentage by the second and drop the sign.
questions.onCorrect: 3. Quantity changed by 60% of its average, price by 20% of its average: 60 ÷ 20.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides price by quantity. Put the quantity percentage on top.
That is the change in quantity, not the elasticity. Express it as a share of the average first.
Check your base: use the average of the two quantities, 50, not an end value.

questions.prompt: Ticket sales rise from 35 at £11 to 65 at £9. By how many pounds does total revenue change?
hints: Revenue is price times quantity.
Compute revenue at each price.
Subtract the old revenue from the new.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Revenue goes from 11 × 35 = £385 to 9 × 65 = £585, a rise of £200.

questions.onCorrect: £200 more. Elastic demand means the gain in quantity outweighs the cut in price.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the revenue before the cut. Subtract it from the revenue after.
That is the revenue after the cut. Subtract the revenue before.
That is the price cut. Revenue is price times quantity at each price.

questions.prompt: Elasticity of demand
hints: Use the average quantity as the base for the quantity change.
Use the average price as the base for the price change.
Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 0.25. The quantity percentage is much smaller than the price percentage, so demand is inelastic.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down. Divide the quantity percentage by the price percentage.
That is the quantity percentage alone. Divide it by the price percentage.

questions.prompt: Museum demand is Qd = 200 − 10P. The entry price falls from £11 to £9. By how many pounds does total revenue change?
hints: Find the quantity at each price.
Multiply each price by its quantity.
Subtract the old revenue from the new.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Visits rise from 90 to 110; revenue is 11 × 90 = £990 before and 9 × 110 = £990 after, so it does not change.

questions.onCorrect: None. Revenue is the same at both prices, which is what unit elasticity looks like.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the revenue at one price. Compare it with the revenue at the other.
That is the price fall, not the change in revenue.

questions.prompt: Demand for a firm's product is inelastic. The firm raises its price. What happens to its total revenue?
hints: Compare the percentage change in price with the percentage change in quantity.

acceptedIdeas: It rises
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: With inelastic demand, quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises, so price times quantity goes up.

choices.label: It rises
It falls
It stays the same

questions.onCorrect: It rises. With inelastic demand quantity falls by a smaller percentage than price rises.

misconceptions.feedback: Compare the two percentage changes: which one is bigger when demand is inelastic?
Revenue stays level only at unit elasticity. Here quantity responds by less than price.

questions.prompt: The price of a phone case rises from £8 to £12 and quantity demanded falls from 110 to 90. Find the absolute midpoint elasticity of demand.
hints: Average the two quantities and the two prices.
Express each change as a share of its average.
Divide the quantity share by the price share.
questions.onCorrect: 0.5. A 20% change in quantity against a 40% change in price: inelastic.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ratio upside down. Put the quantity percentage on top.
That is the quantity percentage alone. Divide it by the price percentage.

questions.prompt: A buyer would pay up to £35 for a cup of coffee and buys it at the market price of £20. How much consumer surplus does she gain, in pounds?
hints: Consumer surplus is the gap between willingness to pay and the price paid.
Start from her maximum, not from the price.
Subtract the price from her maximum.
questions.onCorrect: £15. Willingness to pay minus the price paid is the surplus on that cup.

misconceptions.feedback: That is her maximum. Surplus is the part she did not have to pay.
That is the price. Surplus is the gap between her maximum and the price.
Adding them does not measure a gap. Subtract.

questions.prompt: Consumer surplus, in pounds
hints: Consumer surplus is a triangle above the price and below the demand curve.
Its height runs from the price up to the price at which demand reaches zero.
Take one half × base × height, with the quantity sold as the base.
questions.onCorrect: £900. Half of base times height: the 60 cups sold, and the 30 between price and top of the demand curve.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the base only. Find the area.

questions.prompt: Producer surplus, in pounds
hints: Producer surplus is a triangle below the price and above the supply curve.
Its height runs from the lowest supply price up to the market price.
Take one half × quantity × that height.
questions.onCorrect: £450. Half of the 60 cups sold times the 15 between the lowest supply price and the market price.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the height only. Find the area.

questions.prompt: A rule caps coffee sales at 40 cups, below the free-market 60. For the 40th cup, buyers would pay £30 and sellers would accept £15. By how many pounds does total surplus fall?
hints: The lost units run from the 40th up to the 60th.
On each lost unit the loss is the gap between what buyers would pay and what sellers would accept.
Those gaps form a triangle, so take one half × base × height.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lost cups form a triangle with base 60 − 40 = 20 and height 30 − 15 = 15: ½ × 20 × 15 = £150.

questions.onCorrect: £150. The cups that no longer sell were each worth more to buyers than they cost sellers.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is only the height of the lost triangle. Find its area.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 80 − 2P and supply is Qs = 2P. What is consumer surplus at equilibrium, in pounds?
hints: Find the equilibrium price and quantity first.
Find the price at which quantity demanded falls to zero.
Take one half × quantity × (that price minus the equilibrium price).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 − 2P = 2P gives P = £20 and Q = 40. Demand reaches zero at £40, so CS = ½ × 40 × (40 − 20) = £400.

questions.onCorrect: £400. Find the market price and quantity first, then take half of base times height.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the market price, not the area.
Check the height: it runs from the market price up to where demand reaches zero.

questions.prompt: Which area on a supply and demand diagram is consumer surplus?
hints: Consumer surplus belongs to buyers, so look for the curve that records buyers' values.

acceptedIdeas: Below the demand curve and above the price, up to the quantity sold
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Buyers gain the gap between what they would pay and the price they do pay. The demand curve records what they would pay.

choices.label: Below the demand curve and above the price, up to the quantity sold
Above the supply curve and below the price, up to the quantity sold
Below the supply curve, up to the quantity sold

questions.onCorrect: Buyers gain the gap between what they would pay and what they pay: below the demand curve, above the price.

misconceptions.feedback: That area belongs to sellers: it sits above the supply curve.
Below the supply curve is the cost of production, not a gain.

questions.prompt: A £6 tax per cup is collected from coffee sellers. Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P, and supply in terms of the price sellers keep is Qs = 4P − 20. What price do buyers now pay, in pounds?
hints: Sellers keep the buyers' price minus the tax.
Replace P in the supply equation by (P − 6) and set it equal to demand.
Solve for the buyers' price.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sellers keep P − 6, so 100 − 2P = 4(P − 6) − 20 gives 144 = 6P and P = £24.

questions.onCorrect: £24. Replace P with P − 6 in supply, set it equal to demand and solve for the buyers' price.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price sellers keep. The question asks what buyers pay.
That is the price before the tax. The tax pushes the buyers' price up.

questions.prompt: Tax revenue per day, in pounds
hints: Revenue is the tax per unit times the units taxed.
Use the quantity after the tax, not before.
Multiply the two.
questions.onCorrect: £312. Tax per cup times the cups still sold.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the tax per cup. Multiply by the cups taxed.
That uses the quantity before the tax. Taxed cups are the ones still sold.

questions.prompt: Deadweight loss, in pounds per day
hints: The loss is a triangle between the curves over the units no longer sold.
Its height is the tax wedge and its base is the fall in quantity.
Take one half × base × height.
questions.onCorrect: £24. Half of the tax times the fall in quantity.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the base only. Find the area.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 120 − 4P and supply is Qs = 2P − 30. A £6 tax is collected from sellers. By how many pounds does the price buyers pay rise?
hints: Find the equilibrium price without the tax.
Find the buyers' price with the tax by replacing P with (P − 6) in supply.
Subtract the first price from the second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Without the tax 150 = 6P gives £25. With it, 120 − 4P = 2(P − 6) − 30 gives 162 = 6P, so £27: a rise of £2.

questions.onCorrect: £2. Buyers who can easily walk away bear less of the tax.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price before the tax. Find how much it rises.
That is the price after the tax. The question asks for the rise.
That is the whole tax. Buyers' price rises by less than that.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 90 − 3P and supply is Qs = 3P − 30. A £4 tax is collected from sellers. How many units are traded after the tax?
hints: Replace P in the supply equation by the price sellers keep.
Solve for the buyers' price.
Substitute that price into demand.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 90 − 3P = 3(P − 4) − 30 gives 132 = 6P, so buyers pay £22 and Q = 90 − 66 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: 24 units. Find the buyers' price with the tax, then put it into demand.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the buyers' price. Substitute it into demand to find the quantity.
That is the quantity before the tax. The tax reduces trade.

questions.prompt: Without a tax 30 units are traded; a £4 per-unit tax cuts trade to 24 units. Both curves are straight lines. What is the deadweight loss, in pounds?
hints: Identify the units that are no longer traded.
The triangle's height is the tax per unit.
Take one half × base × height.
questions.onCorrect: £12. Half of the tax per unit times the units no longer traded.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the fall in quantity only. Find the area of the triangle.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P and supply is Qs = 4P − 20. A price ceiling of £12 is imposed. How large is the shortage, in cups?
hints: A ceiling below equilibrium is the price that actually applies.
Find quantity demanded and quantity supplied at the ceiling.
Subtract supply from demand.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At £12, Qd = 100 − 24 = 76 and Qs = 48 − 20 = 28, so the shortage is 76 − 28 = 48 cups.

questions.onCorrect: 48 cups. At the ceiling buyers want 76 and sellers offer 28: the gap is the shortage.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what buyers want. Subtract what sellers offer.
That is what sellers offer. The shortage is the gap between the two quantities.
That is the quantity at equilibrium. At the ceiling the two quantities differ.

questions.prompt: Cups offered but not bought
hints: A floor above equilibrium holds the price at the floor.
Find both quantities at the floor.
Subtract demand from supply.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At £30, Qs = 120 − 20 = 100 and Qd = 100 − 60 = 40: 60 cups go unsold.

questions.onCorrect: 60 cups. At a floor above equilibrium sellers offer more than buyers take.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what sellers offer. Subtract what buyers take.
That is what buyers take. Subtract it from what sellers offer.

questions.prompt: A paint market has demand Qd = 100 − 2P and supply Qs = 4P − 20, where supply reflects firms' own costs. Each tonne also causes £9 of pollution damage to people nearby. What quantity, in tonnes, maximises total surplus once that damage is counted?
hints: Add the external cost to the firms' own cost of each tonne.
In the supply equation, that means replacing P by (P − 9).
Set that social supply equal to demand and solve for quantity.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Social supply is 4(P − 9) − 20. Setting it equal to 100 − 2P gives 156 = 6P, so P = £26 and Q = 100 − 52 = 48 tonnes.

questions.onCorrect: 48 tonnes. Add the damage to each tonne's cost, then meet demand.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the market quantity, which ignores the damage.
That is the price, not the quantity.

questions.prompt: In that paint market 60 tonnes are produced instead of the efficient 48, and each tonne does £9 of damage. What is the deadweight loss of the unregulated market, in pounds?
hints: The loss comes only from the overproduced tonnes.
On those tonnes the gap between social cost and value grows from zero to the external cost.
Take one half × base × height.
questions.onCorrect: £54. Over the overproduced tonnes the gap grows from nothing to the damage per tonne: a triangle.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the base only. Find the area.

questions.prompt: A price ceiling of £30 is set in a market whose equilibrium price is £20. What happens?
hints: Ask whether the legal maximum stops the market price being reached.

acceptedIdeas: The ceiling does not bind, and nothing changes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The market price of £20 is already below the £30 maximum, so the ceiling has no effect.

choices.label: The ceiling does not bind, and nothing changes
A shortage appears
A surplus appears

questions.onCorrect: Nothing changes. A ceiling above the equilibrium price never stops the market reaching it.

misconceptions.feedback: A shortage needs the ceiling to sit below the price the market would reach.
A surplus comes from a floor above equilibrium, not from a ceiling.

questions.prompt: A per-unit tax set equal to the marginal external cost of an activity is named after which economist? Surname only.
hints: He succeeded Alfred Marshall as professor of political economy at Cambridge.

acceptedIdeas: Pigou
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Pigou: Arthur Cecil Pigou, in The Economics of Welfare (1920).

questions.onCorrect: Pigou. A tax equal to the marginal external cost is called a Pigouvian tax.

questions.prompt: A firm's total cost is TC = 100 + q², where £100 is fixed. What is average total cost at q = 5, in pounds?
hints: Average total cost is total cost divided by output.
Find total cost at that output first.
Divide by the number of units.
questions.onCorrect: £25. Total cost is 100 + 25 = 125; divide by 5 units.

misconceptions.feedback: That is total cost. Divide by the output.
That is the output, not the cost per unit.
That shares only the rent over 5 units. The other cost counts too.

questions.prompt: Output with the lowest average cost
hints: Average cost falls while the next unit costs less than the average.
The lowest point is where marginal cost equals average total cost.
Set the two expressions equal and solve for q.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: ATC is lowest where MC = ATC: 2q = 100/q + q gives q² = 100, so q = 10.

questions.onCorrect: 10 units. Where MC meets ATC, average cost stops falling.

misconceptions.feedback: That is q squared. Take the square root.
That is the average cost at the lowest point, not the output.

questions.prompt: A competitive firm with MC = 2q sells at a market price of £30. What output maximises its profit?
hints: A price-taker's marginal revenue equals the price.
Produce while the next unit's revenue covers its marginal cost.
Solve price = 2q.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Marginal revenue is the £30 price; 30 = 2q gives q = 15.

questions.onCorrect: 15 units. A price-taker produces until marginal cost rises to meet the price.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the slope. Divide the price by the slope instead.
That is the price, not the output.

questions.prompt: A firm has total cost TC = 100 + q² and sells 15 units at £30 each. What is its profit, in pounds?
hints: Profit is total revenue minus total cost.
Revenue is price times quantity.
Total cost includes the fixed £100.
questions.onCorrect: £125. Revenue less total cost, rent included.

misconceptions.feedback: That is revenue. Subtract total cost.
That is total cost. Subtract it from revenue.

questions.prompt: Total cost is £50 at 0 units, £70 at 1, £85 at 2, £105 at 3 and £135 at 4. What is the marginal cost of the third unit, in pounds?
hints: Marginal cost is the change in total cost from one more unit.
Compare total cost at 2 units and at 3 units.
Subtract the smaller total from the larger.
questions.onCorrect: £20. Marginal cost is the change in total cost from one more unit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total cost at three units. Marginal cost is the change from the unit before.
That is the average cost at three units. Marginal cost is only the extra for the third.
That is the extra cost of the fourth unit. Look at the third.

questions.prompt: A competitive firm sells at £50 and its marginal cost is MC = 10 + 2q. What output maximises profit?
hints: Set price equal to marginal cost.
Move the constant to one side.
Divide by the slope of the marginal cost line.
questions.onCorrect: 20 units. Set price equal to marginal cost, then solve.

misconceptions.feedback: That is price minus the constant. Divide by the slope as well.
That ignores the constant in marginal cost.

questions.prompt: A monopolist faces demand P = 100 − Q, so marginal revenue is MR = 100 − 2Q. What is marginal revenue at Q = 30, in pounds?
hints: Substitute the quantity into the MR equation.
Double the quantity first.
Subtract that from the intercept.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: MR = 100 − 2 × 30 = £40, well below the £70 price.

questions.onCorrect: £40, well below the £70 price. A sole seller's extra unit is worth less than its price.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price at 30 units. Marginal revenue is lower.
That is the intercept. Substitute the quantity into the equation.

questions.prompt: Price from the demand curve, in pounds
hints: Find the output where MR equals MC first.
Solve 100 − 2Q = MC.
Read the price from the demand curve at that output.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 − 2Q = 20 gives Q = 40, and the demand curve gives P = 100 − 40 = £60.

questions.onCorrect: £60. Output from MR = MC, then the price demand allows at that output.

misconceptions.feedback: That is marginal cost. Read the price from the demand curve.
That is the output. Put it into the demand curve.

questions.prompt: Demand is P = 100 − Q and marginal cost is a constant £20. If the market were competitive, price would equal marginal cost. What quantity would be sold?
hints: Set the demand price equal to marginal cost.
Solve 100 − Q = MC.
Compare the result with the monopoly output.
questions.onCorrect: 80 units. Competition pushes price down to marginal cost, so the monopoly output is only half this.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the monopoly output. Competition sets price equal to marginal cost.
That is the price. The question asks for the quantity.

questions.prompt: In that market a monopoly sells 40 units at £60, while competition would sell 80 units at £20. What is the monopoly's deadweight loss, in pounds?
hints: The lost units lie between the two quantities.
On them, the gap between buyers' value and marginal cost shrinks from the markup to zero.
Take one half × base × height.
questions.onCorrect: £800. The 40 units never sold were each worth more to buyers than they cost to make.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the base only. Find the area.

questions.prompt: A monopolist faces P = 60 − 2Q and has a constant marginal cost of £12. What is its profit-maximising quantity?
hints: With P = a − bQ, marginal revenue is a − 2bQ.
Write the MR equation for this demand curve.
Set MR equal to marginal cost and solve.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: MR = 60 − 4Q. Setting 60 − 4Q = 12 gives Q = 12, sold at P = 60 − 24 = £36.

questions.onCorrect: 12 units. Double the demand slope to get MR, then set it equal to marginal cost.

misconceptions.feedback: You used the demand slope for marginal revenue. MR falls twice as fast.
That is the price, not the quantity.

questions.prompt: Compared with a competitive market with the same costs, a profit-maximising monopoly…
hints: Marginal revenue lies below the demand curve.

acceptedIdeas: sells less at a higher price
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It stops where MR = MC, short of where price meets marginal cost, and charges what demand allows for that smaller output.

choices.label: sells less at a higher price
sells more at a lower price
sells the same quantity at a higher price

questions.onCorrect: It sells less at a higher price: it stops where MR = MC, short of where price meets marginal cost.

misconceptions.feedback: A monopoly restricts output; it does not expand it.
It cuts output where MR meets MC, short of the competitive quantity.

questions.prompt: Alpha and Beta each set a High or Low price. If Beta sets High, Alpha earns £10m by also setting High and £14m by setting Low. If Beta sets Low, Alpha earns £2m with High and £5m with Low. When Beta sets High, how many £m more does Alpha earn by choosing Low?
hints: Fix Beta's choice and look only at that column.
Compare Alpha's two payoffs in it.
Subtract the smaller from the larger.
questions.onCorrect: £4m. To find a best response, fix the rival's choice and compare your own payoffs.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Alpha's payoff from Low, not the extra it earns over High.
That is Alpha's payoff from High. Find the difference between the two.
That compares the two payoffs in Beta's Low column. Beta sets High here.

questions.prompt: Alpha and Beta each set a High or a Low price. If Beta sets High, Alpha earns £10m with High and £14m with Low. If Beta sets Low, Alpha earns £2m with High and £5m with Low. Which price is a dominant strategy for Alpha? Answer High or Low.
hints: Find Alpha's best response to each of Beta's choices.
A dominant strategy is the best response to every choice the rival makes.

acceptedIdeas: Low
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Low: it pays Alpha more whatever Beta does.

questions.onCorrect: Low. It pays more against High (£14m to £10m) and against Low (£5m to £2m).

misconceptions.feedback: High pays best only if Beta also sets High. A dominant strategy has to win against both of Beta's choices.

questions.prompt: In the price war between Alpha and Beta, Low is each firm's dominant strategy, so both set Low. What combined profit, in £m, do the two firms earn there?
hints: Find the cell where both firms set Low.
Read both payoffs in that cell.
Add them.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Low/Low gives £5m + £5m = £10m, half the £20m of High/High.

questions.onCorrect: £10m. Both play Low, earning £5m each, half of the £20m that High/High would give.

misconceptions.feedback: That is each firm's profit. The question asks for the combined profit.
That is the combined profit at High/High, which is not the equilibrium.

questions.prompt: Alpha and Beta play their price game for five rounds. Alpha plays tit for tat (High in round one, then it copies Beta's last move) and Beta always sets Low. A lone High pays £2m, a lone Low pays £14m and Low/Low pays £5m each. What is Alpha's total profit over the five rounds, in £m?
hints: Write down both moves for each round.
In round one only Alpha sets High.
Add Alpha's payoff across all five rounds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Round one: Alpha High, Beta Low, so Alpha earns £2m. Rounds two to five: Low/Low, £5m each. Total 2 + 4 × 5 = £22m.

questions.onCorrect: £22m. One undercut costs Alpha once; after that it matches Low and loses little more.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Beta's total. Alpha earns less.
That treats all five rounds as Low/Low. In round one Alpha plays High.
That is what Alpha would earn if Beta cooperated every round. Beta always sets Low.

questions.prompt: Number of Nash equilibria
hints: Check each of the four cells in turn.
In each cell, ask whether either maker gains by switching alone.
Count the cells where neither does.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A/A and B/B are both equilibria: in each, switching alone drops a maker to nothing. The mismatched cells are not.

questions.onCorrect: 2 equilibria. A/A and B/B are both stable; the mismatched cells are not.

misconceptions.feedback: Check every cell, not just the best-paying one.
The mismatched cells are not equilibria: a maker there earns nothing and gains by switching.

questions.prompt: A game in which each player's dominant strategy leaves both worse off than cooperation is called the prisoner's what? One word.
hints: Picture two suspects questioned separately, each tempted to confess.

acceptedIdeas: dilemma
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dilemma: the prisoner's dilemma.

questions.onCorrect: Dilemma. Each player's best choice leaves both worse off than cooperating.

misconceptions.feedback: A paradox is a puzzle; this one is a choice that tempts each player. The word is the one used for the two suspects.

questions.prompt: Cleo can bake 2 cakes or 10 loaves in a day. Dev can bake 4 cakes or 4 loaves. Who has the comparative advantage in cakes?
hints: Price a cake in loaves for each of them.

acceptedIdeas: Dev
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Dev. A cake costs him 1 loaf and costs Cleo 5.

choices.label: Dev
Cleo, who bakes more loaves
Neither: their costs are the same

questions.onCorrect: Dev. A cake costs him 4 ÷ 4 loaves against Cleo's 10 ÷ 2: the lower opportunity cost.

misconceptions.feedback: Baking more loaves makes Cleo's loaves cheap, not her cakes. Compare what each gives up per cake.
Work out each person's loaves per cake. The two costs are far apart.

questions.prompt: Why does Ana end up with the comparative advantage in loaves?
hints: Compare what each gives up per loaf.

acceptedIdeas: A loaf costs her fewer cakes than it costs Ben.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A loaf costs Ana half a cake and Ben two-thirds of one, so her cost is lower.

choices.label: A loaf costs her fewer cakes than it costs Ben.
She is faster at baking everything.
Ben cannot bake loaves.

questions.onCorrect: A loaf costs Ana half a cake and Ben two-thirds of one, so her cost is lower.

misconceptions.feedback: Being faster at both is an absolute advantage. Comparative advantage compares what each gives up.
Ben can bake loaves. He gives up more cakes per loaf than Ana does.

questions.prompt: Loaves received for the 2 cakes
hints: Each cake fetches the agreed price in loaves.
He swaps more than one cake.
Multiply the number of cakes swapped by the price of one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 2 cakes × 1.75 loaves = 3.5 loaves.

questions.onCorrect: 3.5 loaves: the number of cakes swapped times the price of each.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price of one cake. He swaps two.
That is how many loaves he used to bake himself. The swap brings in a different amount.

questions.prompt: Ben's cake costs him 1.5 loaves to make and Ana's costs her 2. Which price, in loaves per cake, helps both?
hints: Each side must do better than making the cake themselves.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 1.8 sits between 1.5 and 2: Ana pays less than baking costs her, and Ben is paid more than it costs him.

questions.onCorrect: 1.8: above Ben's cost and below Ana's, so each does better than going it alone.

misconceptions.feedback: Ben would be paid less than a cake costs him to bake, so he would not sell.
Ana would pay more than baking the cake herself costs her, so she would not buy.

questions.prompt: Lena can make 6 mugs or 24 plates in a day; Sam can make 6 mugs or 6 plates. By how many plates does Lena's opportunity cost of a mug exceed Sam's?
hints: Price a mug in plates for Lena.
Do the same for Sam.
Subtract the smaller price from the larger.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Lena: 24 ÷ 6 = 4 plates per mug. Sam: 6 ÷ 6 = 1 plate. 4 − 1 = 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3 plates. Price a mug for each, then take the smaller from the larger.

misconceptions.feedback: That is Lena's price alone. The question asks how much it exceeds Sam's.
That is Sam's price alone. Find how far Lena's price sits above it.
Subtracting the maximums skips the pricing. Price a mug in plates for each person first.

questions.prompt: A cake costs Ana 2 loaves to bake herself and costs Ben 1.5. They agree a price of 1.75 loaves per cake. Ana buys 8 cakes from Ben instead of baking them. How many loaves does she save?
hints: How many loaves would baking those cakes herself cost her?
How many loaves does she pay Ben for the same cakes?
Subtract what she pays from what baking would have cost.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Baking 8 cakes would cost her 8 × 2 = 16 loaves. Buying costs 8 × 1.75 = 14. She saves 16 − 14 = 2.

questions.onCorrect: 2 loaves. She pays less than baking would cost her, on every cake she buys.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what she pays Ben. Compare it with what baking would have cost her.
That is what baking the cakes herself would cost. Subtract what she actually pays.
That is the saving on one cake. She buys several.

questions.prompt: Three friends would pay up to £30, £25 and £20 for a ticket. Tickets cost £22. Together, how many pounds better off are the friends who buy?
hints: Who is willing to pay at least the price?
For each buyer, how far above the price is their limit?
Add those gaps for the buyers only.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first two buy: (30 − 22) + (25 − 22) = 8 + 3 = 11. The third would pay only 20, so does not buy.

questions.onCorrect: £11. Each buyer gains the gap between what they would pay and the price. The third friend does not buy, so adds nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds up what they would pay. Only the gap above the price counts.
The third friend would not buy at that price, so there is no loss to subtract.

questions.prompt: Why is the triangle's height 30 − 20?
hints: Where does the surplus sit on the price axis?

acceptedIdeas: It runs from the price paid up to the highest price anyone would pay.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Demand reaches zero at £30, and the price is £20. The surplus sits between them.

choices.label: It runs from the price paid up to the highest price anyone would pay.
Thirty is the quantity sold.
Buyers all pay 30.

questions.onCorrect: Surplus sits between the price paid and the top of the demand curve.

misconceptions.feedback: Quantity is on the other axis. The height is measured in pounds.
Buyers pay the market price. The 30 is the most anyone would pay.

questions.prompt: A cup beyond the equilibrium quantity is worth £18 to its buyer and costs £22 to make. Would selling it raise total surplus?
hints: Compare the value the buyer gets with the cost of making it.

acceptedIdeas: No: it costs more than it is worth.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cup adds £18 of value and uses £22 of cost, so total surplus would fall by £4.

choices.label: No: it costs more than it is worth.
Yes: someone is willing to buy it.
Yes: the seller makes a profit.

questions.onCorrect: No. A trade raises total surplus only if the buyer's value exceeds the seller's cost.

misconceptions.feedback: Willingness to buy at some price is not enough. The buyer's value has to exceed the cost of making it.
At a price above the buyer's value no sale happens. At a price they will pay, the seller loses on the cup.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 100 − 5P and supply is Qs = 5P. What is consumer surplus at equilibrium, in pounds?
hints: Find the equilibrium price and quantity first.
Find the price at which demand reaches zero.
Take half of the quantity times the gap between that price and the market price.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 − 5P = 5P gives P = £10 and Q = 50. Demand reaches zero at £20. CS = ½ × 50 × (20 − 10) = £250.

questions.onCorrect: £250. Equilibrium first, then half of base times height.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the market price, not the area.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 80 − 4P and supply is Qs = 4P − 16. What is producer surplus at equilibrium, in pounds?
hints: Find the equilibrium price and quantity first.
Find the price below which sellers offer nothing.
Take half of the quantity times the gap between the market price and that price.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 80 − 4P = 4P − 16 gives P = £12 and Q = 32. Supply starts at £4. PS = ½ × 32 × (12 − 4) = £128.

questions.onCorrect: £128. Half of the quantity sold times the gap above the lowest supply price.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the market price, not the area.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 100 − 5P and supply is Qs = 5P, so 50 units sell at £10. A cap limits sales to 40. At the 40th unit buyers would pay £12 and sellers would accept £8. By how many pounds does total surplus fall?
hints: Which units are no longer traded?
What is the gap between buyers' value and sellers' cost at the 40th unit?
The lost surplus is a triangle: take half of base times height.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The lost units form a triangle: base 50 − 40 = 10, height 12 − 8 = 4. ½ × 10 × 4 = £20.

questions.onCorrect: £20. The units that cannot be sold were each worth more to buyers than they cost sellers.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the base only. Find the area.

questions.prompt: A law forbids charging more than £10 for a concert ticket. At £10, fans want 500 tickets and the venue will offer 300. How many tickets are sold?
hints: A sale needs both a buyer and a seller.
Nobody can be made to sell more than they will offer.
Which of the two figures limits the number of sales?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A sale needs a willing buyer and a willing seller. Sellers offer only 300, so 300 are sold.

questions.onCorrect: 300 tickets. Trade stops at the smaller of the two quantities, and the gap is a shortage.

misconceptions.feedback: Fans want 500, but sellers will offer only 300. A sale needs both sides.
Adding the two mixes up the sides. A sale needs a buyer and a seller for the same ticket.
That is the gap between them, the shortage. The question asks how many are sold.

questions.prompt: Why are only 48 cups bought, not 84?
hints: Who decides how many cups are bought?

acceptedIdeas: Nobody can be made to buy more than they want at that price.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At the floor price buyers want only 48. The extra cups sellers offer find no buyer.

choices.label: Nobody can be made to buy more than they want at that price.
Sellers will only offer 48 cups.
The floor is below the equilibrium price.

questions.onCorrect: Buyers decide how much they take, and at a high price that is less than sellers offer.

misconceptions.feedback: At the floor price sellers offer far more than that. The limit comes from the buyers' side.
This floor sits above equilibrium. That is why it binds.

questions.prompt: Cups offered at the £30 floor
hints: Put the floor price into the supply equation.
Multiply the price by the slope first.
Take the intercept off that product.
questions.onCorrect: 100 cups: sellers respond to the floor price, not to the old equilibrium.

misconceptions.feedback: The supply equation has a number to take off as well. Finish the subtraction.
That is the quantity demanded at £30. The question asks about supply.

questions.prompt: Paint firms ignore £9 of damage per tonne to people nearby. Compared with the efficient amount, the market produces:
hints: Is the cost firms count smaller or larger than the cost to society?

acceptedIdeas: Too much paint.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Firms count only their own costs, so paint looks cheaper to make than it is for society, and too much is made.

choices.label: Too much paint.
Too little paint.
Exactly the efficient amount.

questions.onCorrect: Too much. Firms count only their own costs, so paint looks cheaper than it really is.
